What a New Rebel Alliance Means for Congo. Former President Joseph Kabila has joined a coalition that seeks to challenge Kinshasa “by all means.”
Could AI Disinformation Disrupt the Midterms?. The answers are more encouraging than you might think.
Brazil’s Sovereignty Is on the Ballot. A far-right win in the country’s presidential election would open the door to U.S. military activity on Brazilian soil.
Europe Is Asking the Wrong Question About Russia’s Hybrid War. Leaders are debating what to call it—rather than what to do.
Netanyahu Vows to Overthrow Iranian Regime. The directive comes as Israel prepares for an election and fresh joint strikes on Iran.
Trump Puts His Faith in Putin. Trump wants a foreign-policy win, but Moscow is unlikely to deliver.
Hegseth Could Face Impeachment if Democrats Win in November. One lawmaker lays out the case for indicting the defense secretary.
Bolivia and Chile Make Nice. The two countries are mending ties after a decades-long territorial dispute.
What’s Behind Turkish-Azerbaijani Tensions?. A fight over veiling reflects deeper strains over sovereignty.
Why the ‘Odds of Mischief Are High’ in These Midterms. Is the United States destined for a repeat of Jan. 6 every election now?
What in the World?. Test yourself on the week of Oct. 17: French protests intensify, Israeli police make arrests, and Trump tempts voters.
How to Make a Monster. What a novel about Ireland’s last great auks reveals about xenophobia today.
Filming Among the Rubble of Nazi Germany. How Hollywood captured the struggle to make a better world.
Why Putin’s Defenders Are Increasingly American. Like Joseph Stalin’s Western fans, they use a vicious foreign regime to grind their axe at home.
The Real Danger of Big Tech. The biggest risks of AI and other advanced technologies have less to do with their growing power than the men behind them.
Netanyahu Orders Large-Scale Military Operation in West Bank. Israeli forces will go “house to house” after two soldiers were killed in a shooting.

Iran Air chief says 30 to 40 operational aircraft destroyed in war. Between 30 and 40 of Iran’s operational aircraft were destroyed during the war, while another 70 to 80 were hit, Iran Air chief executive Taher Abdolhai said on Monday.

Saudi Arabia should join US-led push for change in Iran, analyst says. Saudi Arabia should join forces with the United States, Israel and the United Arab Emirates to help bring about political change in Iran, rather than continue policies that have failed to contain Tehran's regional influence, an analyst told Iran International.

Iran-Pakistan border trade halt leaves trucks and cargo stranded. Trade between Iran and Pakistan remained suspended at two major border crossings on Tuesday, leaving trucks and cargo stranded, with Pakistani authorities citing security and anti-smuggling measures and Iran pointing to technical difficulties.

Toppling Iran’s regime is ‘primary objective,’ Netanyahu says after US talks. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Tuesday that toppling Iran’s regime was Israel’s “primary objective,” a day after discussing Iran with US War Secretary Pete Hegseth during an unannounced visit to Israel.

Pakistani mediator leaves Tehran after Iran doubles down on demands. Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir left Tehran on Tuesday after Iranian leaders reiterated their conditions for negotiations with Washington and ruled out transferring enriched nuclear material abroad, as regional mediators continue efforts to ease the standoff.

Iran in Israeli election: Netanyahu all-in on regime change, rivals want more. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is making regime change in Iran an explicit goal ahead of Israel’s election, while political rivals advocate tough measures against Tehran and criticize his failure to eliminate the Iranian threat.

Iran hardliners split over role of mediators in US tensions. Renewed efforts to avert another war with the United States drew conflicting responses in Tehran, with hardliners questioning mediators’ motives while officials defended keeping diplomatic channels open.

Iran accused of stoking French unrest through influence operations. Iran is seeking to amplify unrest in France through online influence campaigns and alleged links to hard-left groups, The Times reported on Tuesday, citing researchers who accused Tehran and Moscow of exploiting student protests to weaken Western democracies.

Ghalibaf allies seek an end to war without giving up leverage over US. A current within Iran’s conservative establishment associated with Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf favors maintaining military and economic leverage while keeping open the possibility of a negotiated end to the war with the United States.

Iranian women killed by relatives after seeking divorce or refusing marriage. Asking for a divorce, refusing a marriage, speaking to a man she did not know: in Iran, each has preceded the killing of a woman or girl by her own family, according to a Shargh daily investigation that counted at least 38 dead in two months.

Iranian applicants protest German visa delays in Tehran. Iranians seeking German work and vocational-training visas protested outside the German Embassy in Tehran on Tuesday over lengthy delays in securing appointments, with some saying they had already lost job offers or training places while waiting.

IRGC threatens undersea cables, but can it disrupt global internet?. The Revolutionary Guards' threat to target undersea internet cables in the Strait of Hormuz raises questions about its feasibility, as the waterway carries a fraction of global bandwidth and damaging its cables would not shut down the world's internet.

Land subsidence threatens villages and farms in southeast Iran. Land in parts of Iran’s southeastern Kerman province is sinking by as much as 40 centimeters a year, with ground fissures advancing toward villages, homes and orchards, according to data cited on Wednesday by the semi-official Mehr news agency.

Russia steps between Iran and US, but how far can it go?. Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed Iran with US envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday and offered Moscow’s help, shortly after Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov visited Tehran as Russia seeks a role in efforts to end the Iran-US conflict.

Canada orders Iranian man deported over role in sanctions evasion. Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board has ordered the deportation of an Iranian man living in Toronto over his role in a criminal network that helped Iran evade international sanctions, Global News reported Wednesday, citing a 36-page ruling.

Iran's jailed twin sisters shortlisted for EU's Sakharov Prize. Iranian twin sisters, one sentenced to death and the other to 36 years in prison over January's anti-government protests, have been named among three finalists for the European Parliament's 2026 Sakharov Prize.

US sanctions law firm, shipping operators over Iran trade. The United States on Wednesday sanctioned a law firm, shipping operators and maritime logistics companies accused of helping Iran evade restrictions on its oil and other exports.

Iraq plays down Iran border disruption as more closures reported. Conflicting accounts emerged Wednesday over Iraq's plans for its border with Iran, as Baghdad attributed the closure of one major crossing to technical shortcomings while reports said more could be shut amid US pressure to restrict trade routes with Tehran.

Israel bars United Airlines pilot over alleged Iran links - Ynet. Israel has barred a United Airlines pilot of Iranian descent from serving on flights to the country over unverified social media allegations that he supported Iran's government, the Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah, Ynet reported Wednesday.

War warnings and talk of diplomacy compete in Tehran. Iranian leaders raised the conditions for negotiations with the United States and issued fresh warnings of a wider military response on Wednesday, even as signs persisted that Tehran was leaving room for diplomacy.

Iran plot suspect says he discussed journalists at London embassy. A man accused of plotting an attack on Iran International journalists told a London court Wednesday that he met an alleged Revolutionary Guards contact at the Iranian embassy while he was gathering information on the journalists.

Iran upholds protester's death sentence over $56 property damage. Iran's Supreme Court has upheld the death sentence of a protester arrested during the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom movement over an explosion that his lawyer says caused about $56 in property damage, the Emtedad news channel reported Wednesday.

German regulator orders liquidation of Bank Saderat Iran’s Hamburg branch. Germany’s financial regulator BaFin said on Thursday that Bank Saderat Iran’s Hamburg branch had lost its banking license and must be wound up. The branch, which operated in Hamburg and Frankfurt, is no longer allowed to conduct banking business.

US blockade leaves Iran with millions of tons of surplus LPG. Iran's LPG exports have collapsed since the US naval blockade began in mid-July, leaving Tehran to find domestic uses for millions of tons of propane and butane that would normally be sold abroad.

‘Living in despair’: uncertainty, economic turmoil erode hope in Iran. Repeated economic and political crises are eroding Iranians' belief that their lives can improve, with official figures showing declining social capital, widespread perceptions of injustice and deepening distrust of the government.

Iran plot suspect says he was told to break journalist’s arms and legs. A man accused of plotting attacks on Iran International journalists told a London court on Thursday that his Iranian handlers had instructed him to break one journalist’s arms and legs and assault another to stop him from criticizing the Islamic Republic.

China values Iran but won't pay any price to defend it. China regards its relationship with Iran as largely transactional and is not firmly committed to defending the current Iranian government, according to Tong Zhao, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Iran’s trade squeeze spreads from sea to land. Border closures and transit disruptions involving Pakistan, Iraq and Turkey are raising fears that Iran’s remaining trade routes could be further restricted, deepening the impact of US maritime and air restrictions.

Iran is running out of economic escape routes. Iran’s options for financing trade are narrowing under a US maritime blockade that is squeezing oil revenue, while efforts to freeze Iranian cryptocurrency funds are putting alternative channels for moving money under pressure.

Istanbul meeting: A new division of labor in the Iran war?. Turkey will host the foreign ministers of seven countries on Friday for talks on the Iran-US war, security in the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab, developments in Yemen and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Once US blockaded Iran, China’s ‘Malaysian’ oil imports dried up. China's imports of oil recorded as Malaysian have plunged alongside the collapse of Iranian exports under the US naval blockade, suggesting how heavily Iran relied on relabeling its crude for its biggest customer.

Iranian state-linked hackers used US server to target dissidents, researchers say. An Iranian state-sponsored hacking group used command-and-control infrastructure hosted in the United States this year after a months-long pause in operations, according to cybersecurity firm Semperis.

Reform UK donor had ties to Iran supreme leader-linked foundation - Guardian. A billionaire donor to Britain’s Reform UK party was previously involved in a business venture with Astan Quds Razavi, a powerful Iranian religious foundation under the authority of the country’s supreme leader, the Guardian reported.

US says it can sustain Iran blockade for ‘foreseeable future’. The United States is tightening economic pressure on Iran to bolster efforts to reach a diplomatic solution and can sustain its naval blockade for the foreseeable future, the US Ambassador to the UN said, as President Donald Trump weighs renewed strikes after midterm elections.

Iran International’s Maryam Rahmati wins UN correspondents association award. Iran International’s New York correspondent Maryam Rahmati has won bronze in the broadcast journalism category of the 2026 United Nations Correspondents Association awards, the association announced.

Iran’s evasion network survives, but the crude feeding it has run dry. Iran still has the knowhow, middlemen and shadow-fleet infrastructure it spent years developing to sell sanctioned oil to China. But it has now run out of oil outside Iran to put through that system.

More patrols, slower internet suggest Tehran is bracing for trouble. Armed security forces and checkpoints have become more visible across Iran, according to witness reports sent to Iran International, while internet access has deteriorated amid fears of fresh unrest and another round of war.

Salvation or tragedy? Iranians debate prospect of another war. Escalating war rhetoric from Iran, the United States and Israel, coupled with military movements across the region, has heightened fears of another conflict, as Iranians debate online whether war could bring political change or deepen the country's crises.

US and Iran trade new threats as diplomacy yields no breakthrough. Washington and Tehran traded increasingly hostile threats on Friday, with President Donald Trump raising the possibility of further military action and Iranian officials warning of attacks on regional infrastructure, while diplomatic efforts in Istanbul produced no breakthrough.

US strikes on Iran now serve the blockade. A possible resumption of US strikes on Iran would serve an increasingly economic war, weakening Tehran’s ability to challenge a blockade that Washington appears prepared to maintain for the foreseeable future.

Pakistan talks peace with Iran, defends Saudis against Tehran’s proxies. Pakistan is mediating between Iran and the United States even as it sends troops to defend Saudi Arabia against attacks by Tehran’s allies, placing Islamabad in the conflicting roles of peace broker and military partner to Iran’s rivals.

Baluch insurgency tests the limits of a war-weakened Islamic Republic. Armed Baluch groups in Iran’s southeast are adding one more strain on the Islamic Republic’s security forces just as war has stretched them thinnest, with 18 attacks in the 18 days to October 10, more than in any full month this year.

Israel’s leaders have long wanted Iran’s rulers gone. They differ only on how. In 1987, with Khomeini still calling for Israel’s destruction, Israel’s defense minister called Iran its best friend. Today every candidate for prime minister wants the Islamic Republic gone. Israel’s leaders have changed their minds about Iran’s rulers, but seldom disagreed.

Iran-born former Mossad officer running for Knesset urges end of Islamic Republic. Nazanin Sharifian, an Iran-born former Mossad officer running for Israel’s parliament with Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party, told Iran International that Israel should step up military and economic pressure on the Islamic Republic’s leaders and work to end their rule.

Iranians vent anger over rising costs of slow, restricted internet. Iranians say they are paying more for slow, unreliable and heavily restricted internet after mobile operators raised data prices by up to 40%, with some reporting that their allowances run out unusually quickly.

Iraq faces renewed Iran war spillover despite pledge to stay out. Baghdad’s pledge to stay out of renewed fighting is being tested by reported Israeli jet flights toward Iran through Iraqi airspace, suspected strikes on militia stores reportedly holding Chinese-made air defenses, and drone attacks on Iranian Kurdish opposition bases.

Iran sends conflicting signals on US deal as Trump raises prospect of strikes. Tehran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifted its naval blockade, Iran’s envoy to Pakistan said Saturday, while an IRGC-affiliated outlet rejected such an exchange and President Donald Trump raised the possibility of strikes as soon as “tomorrow.”

From six-day victory to wars of attrition: How has Israel ended its wars?. The war with Iran raises a familiar question for Israel: Can battlefield gains produce lasting peace? Its military history offers mixed answers, from unresolved victories to withdrawals and ceasefires that left adversaries armed.

Iran nearing mental-health emergency, psychology chief says. Iran may be approaching a mental-health emergency as prolonged uncertainty over war, economic pressure and the future takes a growing toll on the public, the head of the country’s Psychology and Counseling Organization said on Sunday.

Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones as Yemen fighting continues. Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over Riyadh and southern parts of the country on Sunday as fighting with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis continued, the Saudi-led coalition said.

Anndal, le nouveau think tank sahélien qui veut défendre la démocratie. Initié par l’Alliance des démocrates du Sahel, un nouvel institut vient de voir le jour, lequel ambitionne de produire une « boîte à outils » de savoirs et d’expertises pour contrer les discours populistes. Explications.

10 choses à savoir sur Mohamed Ould Abdel Vetah, le « Monsieur pétrole » de Ghazouani. Aux commandes du ministère de l’Énergie et du Pétrole, le dirigeant retrouve un poste qu’il a déjà occupé entre 2016 et 2020. Sa mission ? Remettre sur pied un secteur en pleine tourmente.

Charafat Afilal, une voix qui porte au ministère marocain de l’Énergie. Huit ans après une éviction aussi soudaine que controversée, Charafat Afilal retrouve les fauteuils du gouvernement, avec un portefeuille autrement stratégique que celui qu’elle avait quitté. Portrait d’une camarade du PPS qui connaît les rouages de l’administration autant que les chausse-trappes de la politique marocaine.

Un Français soupçonné d’espionnage arrêté en Guinée équatoriale. Arrêté près du Cameroun, l’ex-militaire français est accusé d’espionnage par la Guinée équatoriale. Malabo affirme avoir tracé des échanges avec un groupe d’opposition classé « terroriste » par les autorités équato-guinéennes.

La France a-t-elle vraiment « imploré » Alger d’augmenter ses livraisons de gaz et de pétrole ?. Alors que certains en France assurent que des « ingérences étrangères » sont responsables des violences commises en marge des manifestations du 27 octobre, une autre rumeur, née sur un site spécialisé, fait la joie de la presse algérienne.

Jusqu’où ira l’expansion des boulangeries Paul en Afrique ?. Après avoir franchi le cap des 100 établissements sur le continent, l’enseigne française prépare son arrivée dans cinq nouveaux marchés d’ici à la fin de 2027. Mais elle doit composer avec une concurrence croissante et des contraintes logistiques, réglementaires et monétaires accrues.

Sénégal : les commissions d’enquête parlementaires de Pastef, outil de reddition des comptes ou théâtralisation politique ?. Sous l’impulsion d’Ousmane Sonko, 11 commissions d’enquête parlementaires ont déjà commencé leurs travaux ou le feront bientôt afin de scruter d’éventuels manquements financiers qui remontent, pour la plupart, à la présidence de Macky Sall. Au risque de transformer l’Assemblée nationale en un tribunal partisan ?

Côte d’Ivoire : pour Alassane Ouattara, les promesses mises à l’épreuve. Un an après sa réélection, en octobre 2025, le chef de l’État a inscrit son quatrième mandat dans le prolongement du précédent. Est-ce suffisant pour répondre aux attentes des Ivoiriens ?

L’opposition algérienne démunie face aux invalidations de candidats aux élections locales de novembre. En Algérie, l’opposition dénonce l’invalidation massive de ses candidats aux locales du 28 novembre. Disqualifiés par la loi électorale et menacés de dissolution en cas de boycott, les partis peinent à bâtir un front uni.

Amea, Infinity, Axian… Le solaire ouest-africain attise les convoitises des géants du secteur. Du Sénégal à la Côte d’Ivoire en passant par le Bénin, les grands énergéticiens avancent leurs pions et multiplient les projets pour conquérir de nouveaux marchés. Un mouvement porté par une demande en électricité qui ne cesse de croître.

Au Maroc, le Sahara fait plus que jamais figure de laboratoire de la régionalisation. La décentralisation est à nouveau au cœur des priorités à Rabat, où le sujet a été remis en tête de la liste des chantiers du gouvernement. Un sujet d’autant plus pressant qu’il conditionne l’avenir du Sahara occidental.

Olivier Bilé, l’universitaire qui veut refonder le Cameroun. Après l’échec de l’Alliance pour une transition pacifique (AFP) à fédérer l’opposition, cet enseignant a lancé Kaïros, un mouvement qui veut réunir civils, militaires et diaspora autour d’une « Table ronde nationale inclusive ». Rencontre.

Mustafa Rawji (Rawbank) : « Notre expérience en RDC est un atout que les nouveaux entrants n’ont pas ». Le patron de la première banque congolaise assume la place du secteur minier dans son portefeuille. Il ambitionne toutefois de prêter davantage à d’autres secteurs de l’économie réelle et détaille sa stratégie pour y parvenir.

RDC : « Vingt ans après la Constitution, il y a de quoi dire et redire », estime Guy Loando Mboyo. Le ministre congolais des Relations avec le Parlement affirme qu’il n’y a pas de projet du gouvernement pour changer la Loi fondamentale, tout en assumant de réfléchir à son adaptation.

Emmanuel Macron annule sa visite prévue au Nigeria et au Sénégal. Selon les informations de Jeune Afrique, Emmanuel Macron, rattrapé par la crise sociale en France, a annulé sa tournée prévue fin octobre au Nigeria et au Sénégal. Une décision qui intervient au moment où Paris cherche à relancer ses relations en Afrique de l’Ouest.

Le Parlement algérien convoqué en urgence : s’achemine-t-on vers une intervention au Niger ?. Députés et sénateurs algériens seront convoqués en urgence ce dimanche 25 octobre et, si l’objet de cette réunion n’est pas précisé, tout porte à croire qu’il s’agit de leur faire valider l’envoi de troupes au Niger, en accord avec le pouvoir de Niamey.

Carburant : le Niger cherche des leviers pour sortir de la crise. Confronté à une sévère pénurie de carburants, le Niger a suspendu ses exportations d’essence et de gasoil. Mais, entre hausse des coûts d’importation et bras de fer fiscal avec les pétroliers chinois, il est difficile de sortir de l’ornière.

RDC : entre le référendum de Tshisekedi et la rébellion de Kabila, la C64 cherche sa place. Prise en étau entre deux camps qu’elle rejette, la coalition d’opposition tente d’établir une troisième voie. Ses leaders ont rendez-vous le 25 octobre, à Rome, pour leur première réunion commune avant d’entamer une tournée européenne.

Fatou Bensouda, ex-procureure de la CPI : « J’étais traitée comme une criminelle ». Sanctionnée par l’administration Trump et régulièrement intimidée pour son implication dans plusieurs des dossiers sensibles dont elle avait la charge à la CPI, Fatou Bensouda n’a jamais cédé. De son enfance à Banjul à sa reconversion diplomatique, confidences d’une juriste qui a défié les puissants, et en a payé le prix.

Emmanuel Macron annule sa visite au Nigeria et au Sénégal, deux otages libérées au Niger, les premiers pas du gouvernement El Mansouri au Maroc… Les 5 infos qu’il ne fallait pas manquer. Cette semaine, le Brief de Jeune Afrique revient sur l’annulation de la visite d’Emmanuel Macron au Nigeria et au Sénégal, salue la libération de deux otages occidentales au Niger, analyse les premiers pas du gouvernement El Mansouri au Maroc, décrypte l’alliance entre Air France et Air Côte d’Ivoire et dresse le bilan d’un an de mandat d’Alassane Ouattara en Côte d’Ivoire.

Au Sahel, l’Algérie revient dans un jeu dont les règles ont changé. Après avoir envoyé des avions pour montrer son soutien au régime nigérien fin août, l’Algérie pourrait franchir un pas supplémentaire avec une intervention militaire plus significative. Un rapprochement spectaculaire qui survient après une période de brouille, dans un contexte sahélien qui a fortement évolué et où interviennent beaucoup de nouveaux acteurs.

Raffinerie de Lamu : le Kenya prêt à accorder un monopole sur les carburants à Aliko Dangote ?. Le Kenya négocie un accord d’approvisionnement en carburant avec Aliko Dangote, qui vient de lancer son projet de méga-raffinerie à Lamu. Entre promesse de prix bas et risque de monopole, Nairobi hésite à lui concéder l’exclusivité du marché intérieur.

La fabrique de l’info : les dessous de l’enquête sur la guerre des drones au Mali. Jeune Afrique vous dévoile les coulisses de son enquête sur les attaques de drones au Mali, des frappes menées par l’armée et les Russes d’Africa Corps. Pendant six mois, des preuves ont été récoltées pour tenter de vérifier méticuleusement chacun de ces bombardements, dont au moins un quart fait des victimes civiles.

Est de la RDC : comment l’AFC/M23 s’est enrichi grâce au business de la bière. Les rebelles soutenus par le Rwanda engrangent des millions grâce au commerce de la bière en RDC, favorisant les brasseries rwandaises tout en étouffant leurs concurrents burundais. Décryptage en infographies.

Au Sénégal, Pastef rejette le budget rectificatif. Alors que le pays fait face à une dette équivalente à 132 % du PIB, le parti d’Ousmane Sonko a rejeté le budget rectificatif en commission. Il dénonce notamment les coupes dans les dépenses sociales et appelle à la protection du pouvoir d’achat des Sénégalais.

Élections de mi-mandat aux États-Unis : ce qu’une victoire démocrate changerait pour l’Afrique. Des coupes dans l’aide internationale aux accords sur les minerais stratégiques, une victoire des démocrates au Congrès pourrait compliquer la politique africaine de Donald Trump et renforcer le contrôle exercé sur son administration.

Kabila à la tête du FRN : comment Judith Suminwa a recadré la communication du gouvernement. Judith Suminwa Tuluka a recadré les membres de son gouvernement après les premières réactions désordonnées aux propos de Joseph Kabila. Coulisses d’un rappel à l’ordre.

Égypte : Abdel Fattah al-Sissi assure qu’il quittera la présidence en 2030… à certaines conditions. Le président égyptien, qui a fait modifier la Constitution en 2019 pour allonger son mandat de quatre à six ans, s’est engagé à céder le pouvoir, si toutefois il estime que les candidats à sa succession sont prêts à gouverner.

Sénégal : l’hôtel Terrou-Bi veut mettre Dakar sur la carte du tourisme international. Avec 30 millions d’euros d’investissements, la reprise de l’ancien Radisson de Diamniadio et des ambitions régionales, le Terrou-Bi entend s’imposer comme une référence de l’hôtellerie de luxe en Afrique de l’Ouest. Objectif final : faire de Dakar une destination de référence, sur le modèle de Marrakech.

Au Cameroun, le bouclier politico-spirituel d’Oswald Baboke, candidat à la vice-présidence. Pasteur et directeur adjoint du cabinet civil de la présidence, Oswald Baboke est cité parmi les favoris à la vice-présidence. Visé par les affaires du faux décret et du trafic d’or présumé, il s’appuie sur un réseau où se croisent membres de la famille, politiciens, hommes d’Église et stars. Cartographie de ceux qui comptent autour de lui.

Chérif Ould Taher, le sulfureux intermédiaire malien derrière les dernières libérations d’otages au Sahel. Enlevées en 2025 par l’Etat islamique au Sahel, une Suissesse et une Autrichienne ont été libérées mercredi. Comme pour un Américain, en août, cet homme d’affaires, considéré comme l’un des principaux narcotrafiquants dans le nord du Mali, a joué un rôle clé.

« Commerçants, femmes, enfants… ils n’ont épargné personne » : plus de 150 civils tués dans une frappe de drone à la frontière entre le Soudan et le Soudan du Sud. Les forces armées soudanaises sont suspectées d’avoir visé un marché transfrontalier bondé de civils, lundi 19 octobre, dans une zone où leurs adversaires, les Forces de soutien rapide, se ravitaillent.

En Tunisie, l’armée tente de ramener les jeunes vers le service national. Longtemps exemptés d’effectuer leur service militaire, les jeunes tunisiens sont rappelés sous les drapeaux par les autorités, qui engagent désormais des poursuites contre les resquilleurs. Des tentatives de recrutements qui s’inscrivent dans un élan de modernisation, mais surtout, de renforcement de l’armée.

Ebola : l’Afrique confrontée à une situation « plus complexe » après la propagation du virus au Nigeria, s’alarme le directeur régional de l’OMS. Au Nigeria, les autorités ont annoncé, mardi, le premier cas de maladie à virus d’Ebola, une diplomate arrivée à Abuja à bord d’un vol en provenance d’Ouganda. Elles ont également identifié 44 cas contacts.

En Guinée-Bissau, un essai clinique sur des nourrissons en partie financé par les Etats-Unis, jugé « contraire à l’éthique », finalement interdit. Proposé par des chercheurs danois et encouragé par le gouvernement américain, l’essai clinique voulait inoculer le vaccin contre l’hépatite B à 7 000 nouveau-nés et attendre six semaines pour 7 000 autres.

Crise migratoire à Ceuta : les services secrets espagnols confirment que le Maroc avait été alerté. Le rapport transmis à la justice par le Centre national de renseignement espagnol souligne la « passivité » des forces de sécurité marocaines lors de l’entrée massive de migrants dans l’enclave, fin juillet. Sans toutefois accuser Rabat d’avoir organisé les passages.

Rwanda : la tenue, « au début des années 2030 », du prochain Grand Prix de F1 dans le pays fait polémique. La compétition fait son grand retour sur le continent africain, et c’est le Rwanda qui a été choisi pour accueillir cette épreuve. Un choix qui suscite des critiques du côté des organisations des droits humains.

Kenya : un immeuble en construction d’une quinzaine d’étages s’effondre à Nairobi, des opérations de sauvetage en cours. Sept personnes ont été dans un premier temps portées disparues après l’effondrement du bâtiment, et les secours sont parvenus à entrer en contact avec certaines d’entre elles sous les décombres.

L’ancien président sénégalais Macky Sall abandonne la course au secrétariat général de l’ONU mais pas ses ambitions politiques. Le 17 octobre, l’ex-chef de l’Etat a annoncé son désistement à la succession d’Antonio Guterres faute de soutien, notamment de l’Union africaine, et à cause de la mobilisation des victimes des violences policières durant son deuxième mandat.

La crise dans le Golfe accroît la dépendance au charbon des pays d’Afrique australe. Le blocage du détroit d’Ormuz a fait grimper les cours du charbon, énergie très polluante mais encore relativement bon marché. Pour les pays exportateurs comme l’Afrique du Sud et le Mozambique, cette hausse est une aubaine, mais elle les éloigne de leurs objectifs en matière de transition énergétique.

Au Sénégal, la colère sociale enfle à l’approche des Jeux olympiques de la jeunesse. Alors que Dakar accueille, à partir du 31 octobre, la toute première édition africaine des Jeux consacrés aux jeunes athlètes, le mouvement social contre la vie chère se poursuit, avec une grève du secteur public qui s’achève ce 23 octobre. Le pays doit aussi œuvrer à apurer les finances de l’Etat dans le cadre d’un accord avec le FMI.

Sur un continent en manque de carburants, le milliardaire nigérian Aliko Dangote veut créer un réseau panafricain d’oléoducs. L’homme le plus riche d’Afrique a racheté 25 % de la société d’oléoducs du Kenya, où il doit construire une réplique de sa raffinerie nigériane. Il poursuit d’autres projets au Cameroun, en Namibie, et entre l’Ethiopie et Djibouti.

Ebola en RDC : un essai clinique du vaccin Tumaini a débuté, selon l’OMS. Face à l’absence de vaccin approuvé contre la souche Bundibugyo, moins courante que la souche Zaïre, la République démocratique du Congo mise sur plusieurs candidats, dont Tumaini, pour lutter contre le virus meurtrier.

Le Sénégal se mobilise pour obtenir la grâce d’une jeune femme condamnée à mort en Arabie saoudite. En 2017, Mbayang Diop était condamnée à la peine capitale, reconnue coupable du meurtre de son employeuse saoudienne, alors enceinte. L’échéance de son exécution approchant, la société civile sénégalaise se mobilise pour obtenir sa grâce, misant sur les relations religieuses et diplomatiques entre Dakar et Riyad.

La raffinerie nigériane de Dangote entre en Bourse, portée par l’envolée des prix des carburants. Une sursouscription est anticipée pour cette opération qui se termine mardi 27 octobre. La mégaraffinerie de Lagos affiche des bénéfices en forte hausse, dans un contexte géopolitique et économique porteur.

La candidature émiratie au poste de secrétaire général de l’ONU fait polémique. Les Emirats arabes unis ont proposé la diplomate Lana Nusseibeh pour prendre la suite d’Antonio Guterres dans deux mois, ce qui soulève de nombreuses critiques, en raison notamment de leur rôle présumé dans la guerre civile soudanaise.

Nigeria : au moins vingt morts dans une attaque de « bandits » dans le Nord-Est. Si cette zone du pays est confrontée depuis longtemps à une insurrection djihadiste, elle est également en proie à des bandes criminelles sans motivation idéologique, qui terrorisent les communautés rurales.

Le Gabon rétablit les réseaux sociaux après huit mois de suspension. Le gouvernement a également rendu l’identification formelle obligatoire pour tous les usagers gabonais en octobre, mettant ainsi fin à l’anonymat en ligne dans le pays.

En République du Congo, les Kabila, rebelles de père en fils. Contraint à l’exil et condamné à mort, Joseph Kabila a pris, le 12 octobre, la tête de la rébellion politico-militaire dans l’est de la RDC, dénonçant la « tyrannie » de l’actuel président, Félix Tshisekedi. Un bagage insurrectionnel hérité de son père et prédécesseur, Laurent-Désiré Kabila.

En Tanzanie, l’opposant Tundu Lissu menace d’entamer une grève de la faim pour protester contre ses conditions de détention. L’homme politique de 58 ans, incarcéré depuis un an et demi pour avoir exigé une réforme du système électoral, était retourné dans son pays en 2023 après plusieurs années d’exil. Il risque la peine de mort.

The information ministry on Saturday rebutted the Afghan Taliban’s stance that it lacked the “capabilities” to fuel insecurity in other countries and criticised it for resorting to “diversionary allegations” instead of preventing the use of Afghanistan’s soil for terrorist attacks against Pakistan. He further contended that the Taliban “do not possess capabilities or resources to foment or finance insecurity in other countries”, and claimed that Islamabad’s “misguided approach distracted Pakistan’s security forces from their own duties”. On Saturday, the information ministry said the Afghan Taliban “once again resorted to diversionary allegations instead of addressing Pakistan’s legitimate and longstanding security concerns”. “Pakistan’s concerns are not based on conjecture,” it asserted, adding that the “assertion that Afghanistan lacks either the capacity or the interest to destabilise Pakistan does not address these documented concerns”. It backed its stance on cross-border terrorism from Afghanistan by citing a report by the United Nations Security Council’s (UNSC) Analytical Support and Sanctions Monitoring Team and another report submitted to the United States Congress. The UNSC team, in its 16th report, “examined the presence and activities of terrorist groups in Afghanistan”, the ministry said. It further noted that the report by the US Lead Inspector General’s Operation Enduring Sentinel for January-March 2026 stated that the Afghan Taliban continued to allow the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) to operate from Afghan territory. The ministry also highlighted other findings from the report, which stated that the Taliban continued to allow TTP “greater liberty and support, resulting in increased TTP attacks against Pakistan”. It added that TTP remained the “largest in number” among those groups. Screengrab from US Lead Inspector General’s Operation Enduring Sentinel’s report for January-March 2026. “The report estimated TTP strength at 4,000–6,000 fighters. These assessments underscore the seriousness of Pakistan’s concerns regarding terrorist sanctuaries and support networks operating from Afghan soil,” the information ministry emphasised. “Repeated attempts by armed terrorists to infiltrate across Pakistan-Afghanistan border, the killing of Afghan nationals and members of terrorist groups during Pakistan’s counterterrorism operations, and the recovery of foreign-origin weapons from terrorist elements, all warrant serious scrutiny,” the ministry stressed. It noted that Pakistan had also raised concerns over “alleged facilitation of terrorist groups by Afghan Taliban officials, including officials in Kandahar”. “Such concerns cannot be dismissed through blanket denials; they require credible explanations and verifiable action.” The ministry further said that “blaming Pakistan’s security institutions does not absolve the [Afghan Taliban] regime of its responsibility to prevent Afghan territory from being used for terrorism against Pakistan”. ‘Legitimate security concerns’ The ministry clarified that Pakistan’s “security measures are directed against terrorist threats, not the Afghan people”. “Attempts to portray Pakistan’s legitimate security concerns and necessary defensive measures as hostility towards Afghanistan will neither deflect attention from the issue nor resolve it,” it stressed. Pointing out that peace and stability were closely linked, it highlighted that Afghan people stand “as much to gain from a region free of terrorism as their Pakistani neighbours”. “The Afghan Taliban regime must end any tolerance, facilitation or support for terrorist organisations, including TTP, BLA (Baloch Liberation Army) and their affiliates, and ensure that Afghan territory is not used to plan, prepare or launch attacks against Pakistan,” the ministry demanded. It declared that Islamabad “will continue to take all necessary measures to protect its citizens, sovereignty and territorial integrity”. The ministry affirmed that Pakistan “remains open to responsible engagement based on mutual respect, verifiable commitments and concrete action against terrorist sanctuaries, support networks and cross-border infiltration”. “However, Afghan Taliban regime must understand that peace can only prevail in the region if Pakistan’s core concern of terrorism originating from Afghanistan is verifiably addressed by the Afghan Taliban,” the statement concluded. Ties between Pakistan and Afghanistan have been strained in the past few years as Islamabad continues to voice its concern over cross-border terrorism. Islamabad has repeatedly urged the Taliban administration in Kabul to dismantle terrorist sanctuaries on Afghan soil, particularly those linked to the banned TTP, that are used for attacks in Pakistan. Officials say those appeals have gone unheeded. September witnessed another bout of conflict between the two neighbours, with Pakistan carrying out calibrated airstrikes in the border region in response to terrorist attacks in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. This was followed by drone incursions from across the border, which Islamabad said were shot down, and two further rounds of retaliatory airstrikes. Pakistan rejects Khalilzad’s allegations of arming Afghans Earlier in the day, the information ministry rejected former United States envoy Zalmay Khalilzad’s “baseless and misleading allegations” that Pakistan was “arming Afghans to fight the Taliban”. Zalmay Khalilzad, then-special envoy for Afghanistan Reconciliation, testifies before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee during a hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, US, on April 27, 2021. — Pool via Reuters The ministry’s response came a day after Khalilzad, who served as special representative to Afghanistan during the first Trump administration, claimed on X that there were “ many reports that Pakistan is arming Afghans to fight the Taliban in Afghanistan”. He further alleged that Pakistan was now “recruiting Afghans to fight against anti-Pakistan insurgents”, adding that ties between the two countries were likely to “get much worse”. “His sweeping baseless assertions merely recycle speculative narratives as part of his personal agenda to prop [the] terrorism-supporting Taliban regime,” the information ministry’s fact-check account said on X. It rebuked Khalilzad, saying his “[peddling] of such unsubstantiated allegations only exposes his skewed agenda-based views”. The ministry highlighted that it was “particularly misleading to conflate Pakistan’s legitimate counterterrorism operations against terrorist organisations operating from inside Afghan Taliban regime-controlled areas threatening its citizens with allegations of recruiting Afghan nationals or sponsoring armed groups inside Afghanistan”. “Pakistan remains at the forefront of the fight against terrorism and has made enormous sacrifices in protecting regional peace and security,” it emphasised. It went on to point out that successive monitoring reports issued by the United Nations had documented the continued presence and activities of terrorist organisations, including the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and Al-Qaeda, inside Afghanistan. “Khalilzad’s allegations conveniently divert attention from the Afghan Taliban regime’s responsibility to prevent its territory from being used by India-sponsored proxies for terrorism against Pakistan,” the statement added. Khalilzad, who negotiated a US deal with the Taliban that led to the withdrawal of Nato forces from Afghanistan, has previously called for Islamabad and Kabul to enter a negotiated settlement multiple times , as recently as January this year . In November last year, the information ministry criticised Khalilzad for “creating a false impression” of the militant group Islamic State-Khorasan (IS-K) having a presence in Punjab. The ex-US envoy had claimed an IS-K commander was killed in Punjab’s Akhtarabad. The ministry later clarified that a man had been killed during a dacoity/robbery-related incident, not a counterterrorism operation, and that there was no evidence linking him to IS-K. In March 2023, the Foreign Office (FO) reacted strongly to a series of suggestions made by Khalilzad, saying Pakistan did not need “unsolicited advice” on the challenges it faces. That statement by Khalilzad also prompted the US State Department to clarify that the former envoy did not represent the country’s foreign policy and did not speak for the administration of then-president Joe Biden.

In Berlin meeting, Siemens affirms support for strengthening Pakistan's healthcare infrastructure. The executive vice president of technology giant Siemens on Saturday met with President Asif Ali Zardari in Berlin and expressed his readiness to enhance support for strengthening existing healthcare infrastructure in Pakistan, the Presidency said. The meeting took place on the third and final day of President Zardari’s official visit to Germany, which came as the two countries are set to mark the 75th anniversary of their diplomatic relations. According to a statement by President Zardari’s office, he was called on by executives from the health company, including Siemens Executive Vice President Daniel Frisch. The executive briefed the president on his company’s accomplishments in Pakistan and acknowledged the difference in health services as a positive outcome of the Sindh health department’s “rationally networked steps”. According to the Presidency, Frisch “expressed his readiness and desire to enhance existing support through innovative solutions and technological applications for strengthening existing healthcare infrastructure of Pakistan”. “The Siemens delegation told the president that their representatives will soon visit Pakistan to sign MoUs (memoranda of understanding) with their partners in capacity building and technological domains in the health industry of Pakistan,” the Presidency said. “The delegation told the president that the technological infrastructure cooperation of the company extends to cancer, stroke and other diseases.” Meanwhile, President Zardari called for the absorption of research-based and technology-driven solutions to improve health services in Pakistan. He affirmed that Islamabad highly values German industrial, technological and infrastructural support from organisations like Siemens’ health division, which has been present in Pakistan for decades, with over 100 employees in three major cities. President Zardari expressed appreciation for Siemens’ presence in Pakistan and noted that the “long-awaited mutual desire of expanded and augmented bilateral partnership” between Islamabad and Berlin was affirmed during his meeting with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier yesterday. He also opined that “affordable, yet qualified and highly standardised health service delivery, stays fundamental to enable each and every citizen to realise unhindered potential”. “We strive for broadened and all-inclusive provision of quality healthcare, particularly for poverty-stricken people in remote areas,” the president was quoted as saying by his office. President Zardari encouraged Siemens to further engage with Pakistan and diversify its investment across multiple sectors across the country. He also assured the company’s upper echelon of the “fullest institutional cooperation” through the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC). Sindh Chief Minister Sindh Murad Ali Shah, Senator Saleem Mandviwalla, the Ambassador of Pakistan to Germany Salman Sharif and Sindh provincial ministers were also present during the meeting. ‘Significant advancement’ in bilateral ties Later, President Zardari departed back home from the airport in Berlin, where he was bid farewell by senior German officials and Sharif. “President Asif Ali Zardari’s visit to Germany, after a hiatus of more than two decades, marks a significant advancement in the bilateral relations between the two countries,” the Presidency said. It expressed confidence that the trip will pave the way for further promotion of goodwill and ties between Islamabad and Berlin. The statement further noted that the high-level meetings between President Zardari and President Steinmeier reflected a “shared commitment to further broadening bilateral relations”. On Friday, Zardari and his German counterpart discussed bilateral relations, with Steinmeier praising Pakistan’s “rising diplomatic profile in the resolution of regional and global disputes”. They also discussed challenges related to Afghanistan, with President Zardari stressing that while Pakistan “has no conflict with the Afghan people”, it would not allow terrorists to use Afghan soil to attack Pakistan’s citizens and violate its sovereignty. Steinmeier appreciated Pakistan for facilitating the verification of 500 Afghans “destined to be repatriated to Germany” and also commended its humanitarian assistance to “millions of Afghans” over more than four decades, President Zardari’s office said. He also took a “significant interest” in the Makkah defence pact signed between Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia, which is aimed at collective deterrence. Pakistan and Berlin formally established diplomatic ties on Oct 15, 1951. Both countries remain actively engaged in the areas of economy, defence, education and culture. Exports to Germany dipped 3.53 per cent to $1.369 billion in the first 10 months of the previous fiscal year (FY2025-26) from $1.419bn in the same period the year prior.

Veto power hinders efforts to end conflicts: UN. • Says geopolitical fragmentation rises as major powers vie for influence • Calls for stronger cooperation on debt, technology, development ISLAMABAD: A new United Nations report has warned that the veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council is one of the reasons multilateral mechanisms have been unable to prevent or stop the growing number of state-based conflicts. The resulting paralysis has weakened decision-making processes, prompting the UN secretary-general to call for Security Council reforms, including an expansion of its membership to ensure fairer representation, particularly for Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, and the Asia-Pacific region. All these voices are underrepresented despite bearing much of the burden of peacemaking in an increasingly multipolar world. The ‘World Social Report 2026’ says geopolitical fragmentation has considerably heightened global risks, with multiple centres of power competing for economic, military and political dominance. According to the report, the number of countries exercising substantial influence in another country has risen from six in the 1970s to 34 today. The rise in geopolitical fragmentation is also evident from the neighbouring countries relations indicator, which has substantially deteriorated since 2008, with 59 countries recording poor ties with neighbours in 2024-25, while only 19 improved. The evolving global order demonstrates a change from two competing countries (like the bipolar world during the Cold War) to a multipolar economic, military and political power structure. In theory, a more multipolar world could strengthen multilateralism, compared to a world order dominated by two competing countries or one superpower. However, the current geopolitical fragmentation and pursuit of strategic dominance risk undermining multilateral processes and global collective actions, giving rise to “minilateralism” or “coalitions of the willing”, the report says. Accelerating climate change, rapid technological advancements and geopolitical fragmentation demand a new generation of development planning that places social inclusion at the centre of economic, digital and energy transformations. The report, prepared by the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs (DESA), says the experience of multilateral cooperation demonstrates that collective action can mobilise resources, strengthen accountability, support social progress, and expand opportunities for development. Renewed international cooperation is therefore essential to addressing structural constraints that exceed national capacities, including debt burdens, financing gaps, digital taxation challenges, technological divides and climate-related vulnerabilities. The report suggests that a renewed multilateral agenda should focus on three priorities. First, expanding fiscal space for social investment through stronger international tax cooperation, improved domestic resource mobilisation, and comprehensive and systematic support for developing countries to reduce the cost of capital and debt service burden. Second, promoting wider access to technology, innovation and digital infrastructure so that developing countries can participate more effectively in the global economy. Third, reforming global governance arrangements to make them more representative, inclusive and responsive to contemporary challenges, thereby restoring confidence in collective action and strengthening accountability to development outcomes. Rising conflicts and geopolitical tensions are weakening international cooperation, disrupting trade and supply chains, and diverting financial and political resources away from development priorities. Not surprisingly, military expenditures are also rising sharply: more than half of countries increased defence spending as a share of GDP between 2020 and 2024, and all nine nuclear-armed states have expanded their arsenals since 2022. As multilateral coordination becomes more difficult, countries with limited fiscal and institutional capacity face growing obstacles in accessing the financing, technology and knowledge needed for digital transformation, climate action and poverty reduction. In low-income and vulnerable economies affected by conflict and fragility, including least developed countries, these are not background conditions but direct constraints on both transformation and inclusion: conflict destroys productive assets, deters investment and weakens institutions, while displacement disrupts education, health services and livelihoods. The report stresses that although economic, digital and energy transformations are reshaping the world at an extraordinary pace, billions of people remain excluded from the jobs, skills, services, infrastructure and social protections needed to benefit from these changes. ‘No-go areas’ do not exist in Balochistan, claims Bugti. Stakeholders see monetary tightening tomorrow. KARACHI: Amid inflationary pressure from costly oil imports linked to the Middle East conflict, economic stakeholders have called for a 50- to 100-basis-point hike in interest rates to curb inflation. The State Bank of Pakistan’s (SBP) Monetary Policy Committee is scheduled to meet on Monday, while the financial market is filled with speculation. However, it was observed that most of the financial experts believe a 50bps hike in the interest rate is imminent. The SBP’s policy rate is 11.5 per cent. Analysts and bankers said the central bank appears to be caught between a rate hike and the long-awaited breakthrough in economic growth. “I am sure of a 50bps increase in the interest rate, but the market requires a 100bps hike to tame rising inflation,” said Rashid Masood Alam, a senior banker. Bankers say 100bps hike needed to tame inflation as Middle East conflict drives up oil import costs He said the looming US attacks on Iran are another factor that may push inflation higher and prompt the central bank to deliver a rate hike. In the first quarter of FY27, CPI inflation stood at 10.2pc, up from 4.3pc in the same period last year. “A 50bps hike looks like the sensible middle ground. Enough to acknowledge the changing risks, without unnecessarily damaging growth,” said Faisal Mamsa, CEO of Tresmark. A 50bps hike may help preserve confidence and monetary stability but the longer-term challenge is considerably bigger, he said, adding that a100bps hike would increase borrowing costs for the government and private sector, with limited additional benefit over a measured 50bps increase. All key central banks, including the Reserve Bank of India, have raised interest rates, while the IMF expects global inflation to reach 4.7pc in 2026, with a 4.1pc projection for 2027. Inflation is proving harder to contain than previously expected. Experts said the government has decided to pursue growth after achieving sustainability, but many factors are against this approach. The primary concern is the escalating war in the region, rising oil prices, and serious problems for both exports and imports as shipping costs reach their peak. A larger hike would make borrowing and investment even more difficult. “Pakistan has become better at maintaining stability, but we also need to find a way to grow without losing it,” said Mr Mamsa. At the same time, the industry is on the other side, demanding a cut in interest rates to bolster economic activity. “Raising interest rates merely in the name of controlling inflation would not prove effective in any way and would turn out to be a failed measure, the burden of which is always borne by traders and industrialists,” said Pakistan Chemicals and Dyes Merchants Association Chairman Saleem Mukati. Korangi Association of Trade and Industry and SITE Association of Industry also demanded that the interest rate be brought down to single digits. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

Pakistan Railways hits panic button after repeated accidents. • Emergency declared, holidays cancelled for officers until Dec 31 • Minister orders removal of operational flaws by year-end • Says health analysis of 1,546 coaches, wagons completed • Deteriorating tracks, faulty rolling stock among causes of accidents LAHORE: In view of repeated derailments and accidents, including a recent incident near Multan that killed and injured several passengers, Pakistan Railways on Saturday declared an emergency until Dec 31, cancelling all public holidays for officers and directing them to address operational deficiencies to ensure safe passenger journeys and freight transportation across the country. “Till December 31, neither I nor the officers concerned will take rest. Until all deficiencies in passenger coaches, goods wagons, locomotives, signalling and other infrastructure are removed, no one in the operations department, including me, will be allowed to avail themselves of Saturday and Sunday as holidays. Anyone found flouting these orders will be taken to task,” Minister for Railways Hanif Abbasi warned while sharing details of the emergency, which came into effect on Oct 24 (Saturday). Under the emergency, aimed at ensuring safe train operations, all kinds of leave, except medical leave, as well as public holidays, including Saturdays, Sundays and other holidays, have been cancelled for officers and officials. They have also been directed to monitor train operations in the field. Railway officers travelling to other cities on official business are required to use trains. Chief engineers of the civil and mechanical departments have been directed to submit daily reports to the ministry on matters relating to their respective departments. The head of the safety department is required to submit a daily report. “It is hereby directed that all officers of Pakistan Railways shall travel by rail for all official tours, and no air travel shall be allowed or reimbursed for official tours. Furthermore, the use of official vehicles for official tours is also not allowed,” read a letter titled “Mandatory Use of Rail Transport for Official Tours”, issued to all senior and junior officers on Saturday. The minister said all dummy (faulty or brakeless) passenger coaches and goods wagons would be removed from service by Dec 31, with all such rolling stock made fully fit for operations. “Parts for coaches, wagons and locomotives, including 36,000 brake cylinders, have started arriving. Officers have been asked to start work on an emergency basis,” the minister said, adding that he was clearing a maintenance backlog accumulated over the past 10 years. “From January next year, all faulty coaches, wagons and locomotives will be fit for operations.” The minister said he would himself travel by train (railcar) from Rawalpindi to Lahore until Dec 31. Similarly, all officers would use trains to perform their official duties. “Air travel will only be allowed for me and the officers in cases of extreme emergency,” Mr Abbasi said, warning officers to remove all deficiencies in trains by Dec 31, failing which he would have no option but to take them to task. He said the health analysis of 1,546 coaches and wagons had been completed, while the inspection of the remaining around 3,000 would be completed by Nov 10. “I have directed the officers concerned that parts which can be manufactured locally should be produced at our workshops. Similarly, I have also directed the officers to meet the demand for concrete and wooden sleepers by Nov 30,” he explained. Several train accidents and derailments have been reported in recent months, including seven in July alone. The major issues identified as causes of derailments and accidents included deteriorating railway tracks, the use of dummy coaches and wagons, the manual point system (kanta system), human error, inadequate maintenance, and a lack of sufficient resources. Dar orders urgent action to rein in rising wheat prices. • Calls for increased market supply, warns against hoarding and speculation • PTI Kisan Wing welcomes wheat support price, seeks effective procurement mechanism ISLAMABAD: Expressing concern over rising wheat prices, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday directed federal and provincial governments to take all necessary measures, including increasing market supply, to bring prices under control. Chairing a cabinet committee meeting to review the stocks, prices and supply of essential commodities, Mr Dar emphasised that safeguarding national food security and ensuring the availability of essential items at reasonable prices were government priorities. The participants reviewed national reserves, procurement frameworks, domestic consumption and price trends. They were informed that stocks of essential commodities remained adequate, ensuring stability in local supplies. The committee was briefed that domestic and imported wheat stocks were sufficient to meet requirements until the next harvest. Regarding sugar, the committee was informed that its price in the domestic market remained well below the targeted retail price of Rs155 per kg, with surplus stocks available until the next crushing season. Mr Dar directed federal and provincial authorities to closely monitor market networks, stressing that all organisations must show zero tolerance for hoarding and market speculation. The meeting was attended by National Food Security and Research Minister Rana Tanveer Hussain, Climate Change Minister Musadik Malik, Special Assistant to the Prime Minister Tariq Bajwa, the secretaries of the national food security and research and commerce ministries, the chief secretaries of all provinces, and senior officials from relevant federal and provincial departments. Implementation urged In a related development, the PTI Kisan Wing has welcomed the government’s announcement of a wheat support price of Rs4,500 per maund (40kg), while expressing reservations about its implementation and demanding concrete measures to ensure farmers receive the announced rate for their produce. A day earlier, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif set the new indicative wheat support price for 2027, increasing it by Rs1,000 from the rate fixed last year. According to a statement issued on Saturday, PTI Kisan Wing Central Secretary Information Khalid Nawaz Sadhraich said the announcement had come after a prolonged wait and persistent demands by farmers’ organisations, which had repeatedly urged the government to protect growers from rising production costs and financial losses. He welcomed the announcement but said its significance would depend on whether the government ensured its implementation in letter and spirit. Merely announcing a support price would serve little purpose if farmers continued to be denied the promised rate when selling their wheat, he added. Referring to previous wheat procurement seasons, Mr Sadhraich said farmers had repeatedly suffered despite government claims and official announcements regarding support prices. “In the absence of an effective procurement mechanism, middlemen and commission agents exploited growers’ vulnerability, compelling them to sell their produce at throwaway prices, often without effective intervention by the relevant authorities,” he said. He cautioned the government against repeating these mistakes, saying farmers could not afford another season of financial uncertainty after investing heavily in seeds, fertilisers, pesticides, diesel, electricity and irrigation. “A support price announced on paper provides no meaningful relief unless farmers can actually sell their wheat at the declared rate,” he added. Mr Sadhraich demanded that the government immediately announce a clear wheat procurement policy, ensuring that it purchased wheat directly from farmers at the announced rate. He said the policy should spell out procurement arrangements and operational procedures and establish an effective monitoring mechanism to prevent exploitation by middlemen and ensure that the benefits reached genuine growers. He also called for the timely establishment of procurement centres, transparent purchasing procedures and an accessible complaints mechanism so that small and medium-sized farmers could sell their produce without unnecessary hurdles or pressure from market intermediaries. Gabd border crossing with Iran reopened. GWADAR: Pakistan reopened its border crossing with Iran at Gabd-Rimdan on Saturday, restoring bilateral trade and allowing stranded trucks carrying LPG and essential food commodities to resume movement after a weeklong suspension that began on Oct 17. Border officials cleared commercial consignments holding a consignment note dated Oct 16 or earlier to cross at the Gabd-Rimdan point, known as Gate 250, in Gwadar. Mir Naveed Jan Kalmati, president of the Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry, confirmed that trade operations resumed on Saturday morning. “Pakistan has opened the border with Iran at Gabd-Rimdan this morning and allowed trucks and other vehicles to move toward Iran and Pakistan with import and export goods,” Kalmati said. Kalmati welcomed the decision, noting that the resumption of cross-border commerce will bring immediate relief to traders and transporters stranded on both sides. He added that the restored supply chain is expected to ease a nationwide LPG shortage and reduce soaring energy and food prices across Pakistan. Saturday’s reopening came after local administrators reviewed the security situation and deployed additional forces to protect trade convoys following an attack earlier in the week. On Thursday, unidentified gunmen had targeted the backlog of freight vehicles parked near the closed Gabd-Rimdan crossing, setting dozens of trucks ablaze and damaging several others. Those trucks had been stranded since Oct 17, when Pakistan’s Ministry of Commerce abruptly suspended trade at both the Gabd-Rimdan and Taftan crossings. The ministry issued a memorandum withdrawing an Oct 3 trade order with immediate effect without specifying a reason for the halt. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

Saudi-led coalition forces, Houthis trade blows; 16 dead in Sanaa, Hodeida. • Houthi media says air raids leave casualties in Sanaa, Hodeida and Mocha • Rebel group claims strikes on Aden, airports, oil installations; Washington warns travellers • Falling debris reported near Makkah, Madina; Two ballistic missiles intercepted en route to Taif, Yanbu RIYADH: Saudi-led coalition forces launched deadly airstrikes on Yemen’s Houthi-controlled capital of Sanaa and the Red Sea port city of Hodeida on Saturday, killing at least 16 people, according to Houthi media. In response, the Houthi forces launched their own attacks targeting Saudi oil facilities, airports and military sites in the southern Yemeni city of Aden. The Houthis’ Al-Masirah television channel reported a series of “Saudi enemy airstrikes” targeting Sanaa and its surrounding governorate, while also reporting around 20 strikes on Mocha. In Sanaa, one strike hit a house, killing at least four people and wounding several others. A separate strike on a residential building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said. In the western port city of Hodeida, Al-Masirah reported that a Saudi strike killed five members of the same family. “Five people, the head of the family, two of his children and his two wives, have been martyred, and his daughter wounded, as a result of a Saudi enemy air strike on the home of citizen Abdulwahed al-Wasabi in the Al-Tuhayta district,” the channel reported. Earlier on Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition announced it had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis toward the western Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence Agency briefly broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western regions, including Taif, Yanbu, Jeddah and Makkah, home to Islam’s holiest city. Residents were instructed to “proceed to the nearest safe place,” and the agency repeated a legal warning against sharing images or information related to “countering missiles and drones.” The alerts were rescinded about 10 minutes later after the agency said the threat had passed. In a post on X, the agency said it responded to falling debris following the interceptions in the Makkah and Madina areas. “Civil defence in the Makkah and Madina regions began to respond to the falling debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles launched by Houthis,” the agency said, adding that some shrapnel fell in Wadi Mughamas outside Makkah. Following the Saudi strikes, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group launched wide-scale attacks targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, an airport in Najran and an airbase in Khamis Mushait. Saree added that Houthi forces targeted an Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery, crude oil pumping stations and the East-West Pipeline. There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities on those reported strikes. On another front, explosions rocked Aden, the interim seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised, Saudi-backed government. Yemen’s Interior Ministry told the state-run Saba news agency that three Houthi ballistic missiles struck coast guard sites, with two hitting the coast guard headquarters and a third striking a building in the Tawahi district. A police source added that a coalition position near the Aden airport was also targeted. Saree quickly claimed the Aden attack, saying Saudi officers were overseeing mobilisation there. “Our armed forces targeted Saudi enemy concentrations at the so-called Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden,” Saree said. US updates advisory On Saturday, the US Embassy in Riyadh and the US Mission to the United Arab Emirates stated that Washington’s travel advisories were updated to reflect an increase in potential armed attacks by the Houthis. Meanwhile, Egypt has suggested sending troops to help defend Saudi Arabia, while Britain and France have offered forces to protect the kingdom. Published in Dawn, October 25th, 2026

Wapda inks Rs133bn deal for Diamer-Bhasha Dam project. LAHORE: The Pakistan Water and Power Development Authority (Wapda) signed an agreement on Saturday with the Power China-IKAN Joint Venture for the Rs133.18 billion hydro-mechanical (HM-1) contract for the Diamer-Bhasha Dam project. According to a Wapda spokesperson, the agreement was signed at Wapda House by Diamer-Bhasha Dam Project Chief Engineer and Project Director Arif Ali on behalf of the authority and Ling Jianke, the authorised representative of the joint venture. Wapda Chairman retired Lt Gen Muhammad Saeed, the authority’s members for finance, water and power, the chief executive officer of the Diamer-Bhasha Development Company, a delegation from the joint venture led by Power China International Group Limited chairman, and representatives of the consultants also attended the ceremony.
