Tamping Down Tensions between Cambodia and Thailand mloukili Thu, 10/15/2026 - 14:47 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Commentary / Europe 15 October 2026 12 minutes Tamping Down Tensions between Cambodia and Thailand Tensions between Cambodia and Thailand remain high, with confrontations continuing along the disputed border and renewed major hostilities a risk. In this excerpt from the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group explains how the EU and member states can help prevent further escalation. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Full Report (en) Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union Cambodia Thailand Fighting between Cambodia and Thailand over disputed territory along the 800km land border killed dozens of people and displaced close to a million more in 2025. Countries from the region helped broker a ceasefire on 27 December, but since then relations have remained adversarial, and there has been little movement toward resolving the underlying conflict. With Thai soldiers holding most of the contested ground as well as slivers of Cambodian territory in four provinces, some 20,000 Cambodians are unable to return to their homes. Phnom Penh decries the troop presence as a violation of Cambodia’s sovereignty, but Bangkok has rebuffed its calls to withdraw. The frontier clashes have raised nationalism to a high pitch on both sides, making conciliatory moves politically costly for both countries’ leaders. The Thai government has declined to reconvene the Joint Boundary Commission, which the parties charged with surveying and demarcating the border, indicating that it is content, for now, with the status quo. Meanwhile, in June, Phnom Penh initiated a compulsory conciliation process under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) to address overlapping maritime claims, after Bangkok withdrew from a 2001 memorandum of understanding on the matter in May. With each side accusing the other of blocking resolution, and periodic confrontations still occurring along the border, major hostilities could easily begin again. Under these circumstances, outside powers have little room to bring about compromise, but the European Union and its member states can do several things to help. Aside from the EU’s general interest in South East Asia’s stability, Bangkok and Phnom Penh are both important, if very different, partners for the EU in the region, and Brussels is keen to ensure that tensions do not spiral out of control again. The EU and its member states should encourage the two sides to resume land border demarcation; offer technical support to the compulsory conciliation commission on maritime claims; and continue support for demining efforts as well as Track 2 and Track 1.5 exchanges. The former meetings bring together non-officials such as academics and civil society figures, while the latter also include serving officials who participate in an unofficial capacity. After two rounds of fighting in 2025 over a longstanding territorial dispute along the 800km land border, a ceasefire between Cambodia and Thailand is under strain, threatened by heightened nationalism on both sides. Source: CSIS Asia Maritime Transparency Initiative; OpenStreetMap / CRISIS GROUP Historical Roots and Domestic Drivers The Cambodia-Thailand conflict is a legacy of colonial-era boundary making that both countries’ elites have long exploited for domestic advantage. French colonial expansion forced what was then the kingdom of Siam to cede territory east of the Mekong River in 1893 and, through the Franco-Siamese treaties of 1904 and 1907, established a border that followed the watershed along the Dangrek mountain range. An accompanying 1908 French survey map deviated from the treaty text, however, placing the ancient Khmer temple of Preah Vihear inside the part of French Indochina that is now Cambodia. Siam did not formally object until decades later. In 1962, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled that, silence in this case being equivalent to acceptance, the temple is on Cambodian territory. This verdict entrenched a Thai nationalist narrative of “territories lost” to foreign hands. After the Cold War, the two countries established a framework for managing their border disputes, including a 2000 memorandum of understanding (MOU 43, for the Buddhist year 2543) that established the Joint Boundary Commission, which has succeeded in demarcating roughly two thirds of the border. A separate 2001 memorandum (MOU 44) addressed their competing claims in the Gulf of Thailand and the joint development of hydrocarbon reserves beneath these waters, worth an estimated $300 billion. Thai nationalists later cried foul about a map attached to that agreement, depicting each country’s continental shelf claims, which they interpreted as placing Thailand’s Koh Kut Island within Cambodia’s claim area. The proximate cause of the 2025 fighting, however, is linked less to historical grievances than to domestic politics in both countries. For two decades, Thai politics has largely revolved around rivalry between ex-Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra and Thailand’s conservative establishment. Thaksin had long cultivated a close relationship with Cambodia’s Hun Sen – who was prime minister from 1985 to 2023, and who is now senate president – that extended to business dealings. When a Thaksin-aligned government moved to pursue joint hydrocarbon development with Cambodia in 2024, conservative nationalists accused the government of “selling out the nation”. The nationalists transferred their antipathy to Thaksin’s daughter, Paetongtarn Shinawatra, when she took over as prime minister in August 2024. Meanwhile, in Cambodia, Hun Sen has been managing a delicate generational transition, ceding the premiership to his son Hun Manet in 2023 while retaining substantial power as senate president. Taking up the Khmer nationalist mantle, though it has historically rested with the Cambodian opposition, Hun Sen has created a climate in which others in the ruling party are less inclined to voice dissent. The Path to War A series of incidents in early 2025 stoked border tensions. A viral video of a Cambodian patriotic gathering at a disputed temple stirred up Thai nationalist sentiment in February, setting in motion the events that led to a firefight which killed a Cambodian soldier on 28 May. Cambodia's decision, in June, to petition the ICJ over four contested areas, including three Khmer Empire-era temple sites, further provoked Bangkok, which insists that this dispute be resolved bilaterally. The rupture between the two states came on 18 June, when a leaked recording of a call between Prime Minister Paetongtarn and Hun Sen revealed her addressing him deferentially as “uncle” and criticising a Thai military commander. The leak precipitated her removal by the Constitutional Court in August for ethics violations. Meanwhile, the Thai military’s hardline stance, including restricting border crossings, won popular support. Formal cross-border trade ceased in late June. Fighting eventually broke out on 24 July, after several Thai soldiers were wounded by landmines along the border. For five days, the two countries’ armed forces traded fire at an unprecedented scale, including Cambodian rocket attacks and Thai airstrikes. Malaysia called on the parties to “stand down”, as did China. Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to suspend trade talks, which were to give the two countries a chance to negotiate lower tariffs, if they did not come to the table. But at least 48 people were killed and some 300,000 displaced before these intercessions produced a ceasefire. The truce proved fragile. Periodic confrontations continued along the border, and a series of diplomatic and technical meetings through October produced only recommitment to the existing ceasefire terms, cemented at a signing ceremony in Kuala Lumpur presided over by Trump, who was keen to burnish an image as peacemaker. But just over two weeks later, another landmine explosion prompted Thailand to suspend the agreement, and a second, more protracted round of fighting erupted on 8 December. Twenty days of fighting killed at least 101 people and displaced roughly one million on both sides of the border, before a second ceasefire was concluded on 27 December, with support from China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The agreement includes provisions for ASEAN observers in each country to help monitor the truce and commits both sides to refrain from reinforcing positions along the border or engaging in provocative action. A Cambodian flag is displayed in front of shipping containers and barbed wire, installed by Thai forces, blocking a road in Chouk Chey village in Banteay Meanchey province on 5 February, 2026. AFP / Tang Chhin Sothy The Present Impasse Since December 2025, the hostilities have given way to diplomatic and legal wrangling, with Cambodia acting far more assertively than Thailand. Phnom Penh has lodged dozens of formal protests with Bangkok, alleging unlawful occupation and characterising the new territorial status quo as a step toward de facto annexation. It has also sought outside scrutiny of Thailand’s actions, raising the border issue in international forums and supporting a July trip to the frontier by the UN special rapporteur on the human rights situation in Cambodia, whose initial findings Bangkok has contested. Thailand, for its part, says it is merely upholding the ceasefire’s provision that troops remain in positions they held when the fighting stopped. It portrays Cambodian diplomacy as an illegitimate attempt to “internationalise” a bilateral matter. It has also organised repeated media and VIP visits to a scam centre it seized on the Cambodian side of the border to portray Phnom Penh as having tolerated transnational scam operations. Three factors sustain this impasse. First, heightened nationalism on both sides makes compromise politically hazardous. Thailand's February election rewarded the conservative Bhumjaithai Party, which had campaigned on a hard line with Cambodia, vowing to keep the border shut and to hold referendums on the memoranda governing border negotiations. Though wary of the risks of renewed fighting, Cambodian leaders also cannot be seen to concede on sovereignty. Secondly, the economic costs of continued border closure, while real, have not proven severe enough to force either government's hand. Thirdly, external powers have limited leverage: Malaysia’s mediation and U.S. tariff pressure were decisive in halting the first round of fighting, but the agreement soon unravelled; China has played a constructive but limited convening role and does not wish to jeopardise its relations with either country by attempting to impose a resolution; and the ASEAN observers, who are dependent on host-country cooperation, have become entangled in the two sides’ competing arguments rather than helping build mutual trust. Cambodia, materially and militarily the weaker party, has sought to invoke international legal mechanisms – the ICJ for the land border and the UNCLOS compulsory conciliation process for maritime claims – making the case that it is the victim and Thailand the aggressor. In parallel, Phnom Penh has sought to manage its own vulnerabilities. After a months-long crackdown, in August it announced the “complete eradication” of large scam centres, in part to counter Thailand’s depiction of Cambodia as a haven for transnational crime. To shore up its standing at home and abroad, the government also appointed Kem Monovithya, daughter of former opposition figure Kem Sokha, to a special ministerial post. Thailand's leadership, having reaped domestic political rewards from the confrontation, sees little reason to negotiate. For its part, Thailand's leadership, having reaped domestic political rewards from the confrontation, sees little reason to negotiate. Bangkok has also moved to unwind the legal architecture underpinning negotiations, withdrawing from MOU 44 (on the maritime border) and vowing to revisit MOU 43 (on the land border) because of its reliance on the 1907 treaty’s colonial-era map. Such a move would further complicate dispute resolution, as MOU 43 provides the only agreed framework for surveying and demarcating the boundary. Bangkok has also delayed on resuming Joint Boundary Commission talks. Its justification for doing so has shifted repeatedly, from awaiting formation of a new government following the February elections to arguing that Cambodia’s pursuit of compulsory conciliation in the maritime domain has “closed the door” to bilateral land border talks, though without offering a legal basis for this logic. Most recently, Thailand has insisted that progress on demining and anti-crime cooperation must precede border survey and demarcation work. This pattern suggests that the underlying obstacle is political rather than procedural, as Bangkok calculates that the domestic costs of delay are lower than those of a negotiated settlement Thais might perceive as conceding ground to Phnom Penh. In sum, the conflict is stuck, with the territorial and maritime disputes no closer to resolution than before the 2025 fighting. Mistrust between Bangkok and Phnom Penh, reinforced by domestic incentives, continues to reward confrontation over compromise. Absent a change in that calculus, there is genuine risk that a local border incident could again escalate into open war. What is at Stake for the EU South East Asia is far away from Europe, and the EU’s interests in the region remain primarily commercial, but the Cambodia-Thailand tensions touch on several broader EU priorities: preventing instability; defending the principle of conflict resolution through law rather than force; supporting ASEAN’s capacity to manage regional disputes; and giving substance to the bloc’s ambition to be a more credible political and security actor in the Indo-Pacific. Thailand and Cambodia are both important to the EU, albeit for different reasons. The EU is Thailand’s fourth largest trading partner, and Brussels and Bangkok are in the middle of negotiating a free trade agreement. They have upgraded their partnership to deepen cooperation in areas ranging from security to investment and sustainable development. Meanwhile, the EU and member states, collectively, are major donors to Cambodia, supporting its expected graduation from least-developed-country status in 2029. The EU has an interest in ensuring that frictions between these two regional partners do not worsen further. ASEAN appears best placed to bring Cambodia and Thailand to the negotiating table, but dialogue has proven elusive. As ASEAN chair in 2025, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim used his personal rapport with leaders in both capitals to help broker two ceasefires, but the bloc’s non-interference principle and its members’ diverging priorities have kept it from playing a more sustained mediation role. Phnom Penh would welcome mediation, including by the EU, but Bangkok is adamant that the dispute be resolved bilaterally. These constraints leave external actors, including the EU, with limited scope to shape the parties’ calculations directly. The EU has repeatedly called for de-escalation, restraint and resolution of disputes through negotiations and in accordance with international law. Brussels has nevertheless sought to use the tools it has. The EU has repeatedly called for de-escalation, restraint and resolution of disputes through negotiations and in accordance with international law. It is supporting humanitarian mine action activities and confidence-building efforts on both sides of the border with a total budget of €3 million and has offered satellite imagery to help monitor the ceasefire. As part of the confidence-building efforts, it is also exploring other avenues for engagement, including a €300,000 initiative, funded by the EU’s Foreign Policy Instruments, to strengthen channels for dialogue among non-governmental representatives in both countries. There are signs that Brussels is looking to do more. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas, who has reportedly taken a particular interest in the conflict, is eager to explore whether the EU could play a more active role in facilitating dialogue between the sides. Her attention was drawn to the issue during visits to the region, when the dispute repeatedly surfaced in her meetings with Asian counterparts. Against this backdrop, her team is considering supporting Track 1.5 (semi-official) dialogue initiatives aimed at rebuilding contacts and creating additional space for engagement between the parties. The EU should be realistic about what such efforts can achieve and how much difficulty it would face in trying to facilitate dialogue regarding a settlement. But that need not preclude a useful role. Precisely because formal diplomacy remains constrained, Brussels could focus on areas where its financial resources, technical expertise, convening power and reputation for neutrality – particularly as compared with China or the U.S. – can help preserve channels of communication, build confidence and create conditions for the parties to return to dialogue. The recommendations below set out several ways the EU could pursue such a role without overestimating its influence over the parties. The EU and its member states should: Encourage the parties to reconvene the Joint Boundary Commission. Given the prohibition on determining international borders by force, codified in Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, there is no alternative to the Joint Boundary Commission’s work of arriving at an equitable border recognised by both sides. To be sure, the EU cannot compel either party to come back to the table, but it should make clear its expectation that both sides will abide by existing agreements, including MOU 43 and the 27 December 2025 joint statement, in which both parties explicitly agreed to resume the Commission’s work at the earliest opportunity. Offer technical and logistical support to the compulsory conciliation commission. Launched in Singapore in mid-September, the Cambodia-Thailand compulsory conciliation process on overlapping maritime claims is only the second such process initiated under UNCLOS Annex V, following resolution of the Timor Sea dispute between Australia and Timor Leste in 2018. A successful outcome will not only remove a trigger for renewed conflict but also bolster international norms, particularly the UN Charter and UNCLOS. The EU, or some of its member states, should make available expertise on maritime boundary delimitation to the commission. Brussels could also offer to host one or more of the commission’s working sessions. Continue support for demining. The EU is already supporting Cambodia and Thailand in addressing the humanitarian consequences of landmine and explosive ordnance contamination and in meeting their commitments under the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention. It should keep pushing for joint demining efforts where possible, as directed in the December 2025 ceasefire agreement, so that this activity can reach its confidence-building potential. Encourage civil society and Track 1.5 exchanges. The EU should also continue supporting civil society exchanges, seeking opportunities to involve officials from both sides to strengthen their effectiveness in building trust. These efforts should encompass development of media guidelines and fact-checking mechanisms to prevent the circulation of false and inflammatory information, encourage people-to-people exchanges and formulate steps toward resuming cross-border trade. Help get diplomacy moving. Given her personal engagement with the issue, High Representative Kallas should offer her Thai and Cambodian counterparts her good offices to facilitate communication between them, including by convening informal discussions on the margins of international meetings. Working closely with ASEAN, she could use these contacts to identify areas of convergence and help the parties find ways around obstacles that are preventing bilateral dialogue from moving forward. In this excerpt from the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group explains how the EU and member states can aid Ukraine and help advance diplomatic efforts. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Full Report (en) Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union Ukraine Russia Russia’s war with Ukraine is escalating. Distracted by its own conflict in the Middle East, the United States neglected its efforts to mediate between Kyiv and Moscow. It finally restarted them in late August after a six-month pause. In the meantime, the warring sides have tried to change the balance of forces. Ukraine has been making increasingly effective use of medium- and long-range drones to strike Russian military, industrial and commercial targets. Russia has responded with round-the-clock aerial attacks to disrupt the Ukrainian economy by hitting port facilities, railways, steel plants, data centres and warehouses. Proposals for de-escalation are on the table, but so far none has received a positive response from Moscow. Relations between Washington and Kyiv have become increasingly strained, with U.S. President Donald Trump announcing an agreement with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to purchase sanctioned Russian oil. Trump has also claimed to have brokered a ceasefire between the sides, though neither appears aware of the details of such a deal. While the administration claims that it is not withholding critical intelligence until Ukraine stops hitting Russian refineries, there are reportedly signs to the contrary. Though it shows no sign of backing down, Ukraine is in a tight spot. Absent a settlement or ceasefire, Ukrainians will face another dark, frigid winter under attack by Russian missiles and drones, with Moscow already signalling that it intends to intensify the pressure it is applying. Meanwhile, the battlefield is expanding. War has returned to the Black Sea, a major export route for both Ukrainian and Russian grain. Russia has also widened the aperture for asymmetric attacks on European Union member states – incidents that may fall just short of full-blown hostilities but nevertheless probe the resilience and vulnerabilities of Ukraine’s friends. In the difficult days ahead for Ukraine, the EU’s support will be more critical than ever. The bloc and its member states rightly see their own security as bound up with Kyiv’s and have become Ukraine’s biggest backers now that Washington has ended material aid. Brussels will need to focus in the near term on helping Kyiv meet its financial and humanitarian needs as well as directing EU defence financing toward Ukraine’s most urgent battlefield requirements. At the same time, European actors should try to reach stronger internal agreement on how to use their sources of leverage with Moscow to facilitate de-escalation while also laying the groundwork for eventual negotiations and implementation of a possible deal. Looking further ahead, the EU should also develop a path for Ukraine’s accession to the bloc that accounts for the possibility of an unresolved conflict or parts of the country remaining under Russian occupation. Local resident Valentina, 86, sits in her flat in a damaged residential building following missile strikes on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv on 2 July, 2026, amid the Russian invasion in Ukraine. AFP / Genya Savilov A War of Attrition Well into its fifth year, Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine continues to take a steep toll on all involved. The ground battle has turned into a grinding war of attrition, defined by heavily fortified positions, drone saturation and slow territorial advances. Both sides are escalating in the air, with strikes deep into the other’s territory. Ukraine’s middle- and deep-strike drones have complicated Russian military operations, damaged oil facilities, degraded other energy infrastructure and jammed up commercial logistics on land and at sea. These strikes have global reverberations. By hurting Russia’s refining capacity, Ukraine has contributed to an increase in the price of diesel oil , which was already very high due to shortages linked to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. The price hike, in turn, has soured Ukraine’s relations with Trump, who is looking for someone to blame as his party seeks to retain control of Congress in November’s midterm elections amid a worsening U.S. economy. As for Russia, in an attempt to weaken Ukraine’s economy ahead of the winter, it has stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian cities, infrastructure and maritime exports, knowing that Kyiv is running out of air defence missiles amid a global shortage of Patriot interceptors caused by the war in the Middle East. Like Ukraine, Russia is taking advantage of rapidly evolving technology – deploying jet-powered drones, loitering munitions and guided aerial bombs in its campaign. The effect has been devastating. Ukraine’s civilian casualty toll is climbing, with the UN registering 1,396 dead and 7,978 wounded in the first half of 2026, up more than a third from the same period in 2025. The peace negotiations initiated by the Trump administration in 2025 stalled for months as the Middle East war ... became the focus of White House attention. As noted, the peace negotiations initiated by the Trump administration in 2025 stalled for months as the Middle East war, launched in February, became the focus of White House attention. In August, CIA Director John Ratcliffe journeyed to Moscow, where he reportedly urged the Kremlin to reach a settlement, warning that its economic and military position could get worse than it is now. Trump’s main negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, resumed their diplomatic track in September, travelling to Moscow and paying their first-ever official visit to Kyiv. Their trip gave rise to hopes that a trilateral format involving Ukraine, Russia and the U.S., suspended since February, might be revived. Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy discussed a possible energy ceasefire in September, and Türkiye, Egypt, India and other countries have pushed for a maritime ceasefire to free up grain exports out of the Black Sea. But diplomacy has since hit another wall. After Zelenskyy condemned Trump’s deal to buy Russian diesel, the U.S. leader said: “It’s time for Ukraine to get a new president”. When Trump later announced that an “energy ceasefire” had been reached between Kyiv and Moscow, neither side confirmed it. Ukraine noted that any such arrangement would have to be mutually observed. While each side is inflicting considerable pain on the other, right now Moscow appears more comfortable with its situation. Kyiv has been keen to reach a ceasefire before the onset of cold weather, as many of its power plants and other infrastructure are still in disrepair after the wave of Russian attacks in the winter of 2025-2026. Moscow, on the other hand, has given no indication of backing away from its demand that Ukraine first withdraw from the areas of its eastern Donbas region that Russia has been unable to seize, as one of several preconditions for a truce. Five Challenges for Kyiv Despite its successes with drones, Kyiv faces major challenges, especially as the fighting drags on. The first is that it has too few air defence missiles to repel large Russian air raids. According to Ukrainian sources, Russia can fire dozens of ballistic and cruise missiles at a time and aspires to increase that number to 200. In the meantime, Ukraine’s supplies of Patriot interceptors have dwindled: in the first half of the year, Kyiv received a third of the interceptors it obtained during the same period in 2025, according to Zelenskyy . In August, Ukraine’s air force announced that it would stop publishing exact numbers of Russian ballistic missiles launched and shot down. Zelenskyy has sought to find more interceptors wherever possible and lobbied Trump to get a licence to produce Patriots in Ukraine. After their latest meeting in September, Zelenskyy said Trump had made a “final decision” on the Patriots, though no word of an agreement has emerged. A second challenge lies on the battlefield and in the ranks of the enlisted. Determined to take over all of Donbas, the Kremlin has relentlessly pressed its assaults on the “fortress belt” of cities still under Kyiv’s control. Ukraine has launched a counteroffensive to relieve pressure on the strongholds of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, but it faces a shortage of personnel under arms. While Ukrainian drone teams have been able to inflict staggering casualties on Russian forces, Kyiv is struggling to find the infantry to hold the line and, where possible, push back the invaders. Ukraine must mobilise at least 30,000 people per month, according to Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov. It will be a tall order. Conscription is one of the most contentious issues in domestic politics, amid reports of corrupt draft officers, desertion and inhumane treatment in the army. Third is the war’s economic cost. As Ukraine hit Russian supply vessels headed to Crimea in the Azov Sea and Black Sea, Russia retaliated with increased attacks on shipping out of the port of Odesa, in effect closing the Black Sea as an export route for Ukrainian grain and metals. Overland and river routes cannot compensate for the volumes of grain transported by sea from both countries. With Black Sea commerce again shut down, there is growing concern about the global grain supply. On top of these challenges, Zelenskyy has said a $27 billion gap looms in Ukraine’s defence funding for 2026. The escalation in the conflict threatens global food supplies, as the Black Sea, a key export route for Ukrainian and Russian grain, has essentially been closed off. Source: LiveUAmap, as of 9 October 2026; Crisis Group research; OpenStreetMap / CRISIS GROUP Ukraine’s fourth conundrum is how to avoid a humanitarian catastrophe as cold weather approaches. In the winter of 2025-2026, Russia deliberately knocked out energy infrastructure, leaving millions of Ukrainians without heat or electricity as outdoor temperatures dropped unusually low. Only part of the damaged capacity has been restored. Putin himself has said the Russian military has been instructed to conduct mass strikes on Ukrainian energy officials. Fifthly, and finally, Ukraine must find a way to maintain political stability. In July, Zelenskyy abruptly fired his government, including the popular defence minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, whom the president said was locked in an untenable conflict with Ukraine’s top generals. Fedorov’s sacking sparked protests across Ukraine. When it became clear that Zelenskyy would not reinstate him, Fedorov called for elections, breaking with the national consensus that voting in wartime is impossible for legal, logistical and military reasons. While Zelenskyy managed to push through a new cabinet, the uproar over Federov’s departure is a reminder that the country’s socio-political cohesion might fray after the war is over – if not before. Meanwhile, a long-running corruption investigation continues to implicate members of Zelenskyy’s entourage. Making the EU’s Voice Heard As Ukraine struggles with these challenges, Europeans sit on pins and needles, knowing that what happens in the war will have major ramifications for their future security. If Moscow wins, accomplishing its goal of crimping Ukrainian sovereignty, the EU will likely face a hostile, emboldened Russia that seeks to spread its influence westward, increasing instability and raising the risk of Russian provocations, particularly on the EU’s eastern flank. If Kyiv manages to preserve its independence, even if Russian soldiers still occupy chunks of Ukrainian territory, it may emerge more confident in its own capacity, but the Russian threat will not disappear. In either case, Russia will remain an antagonistic neighbour for the EU, and the underlying Russia-Ukraine frictions will be a potential source of renewed conflict in Europe. The current escalation of Russia’s asymmetric attacks on European states already shows an increasing level of hostility. For all these reasons and others, the EU and its member states have a major stake in any diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the war. Figuring out how to defend that stake has been a challenge. While the EU itself has played no direct role in discussions between Washington and Moscow, individual European leaders have sought to shape the course of negotiations. Since Zelenskyy’s disastrous White House debut in February 2025, European leaders have repeatedly come to his aid in standing up to the Trump administration and helping prevent Washington from strong-arming Kyiv into making a disadvantageous bargain with Moscow. Right now, however, the European role is limited. While several European leaders have bent Trump’s ear at one time or another, the White House has consistently made it clear that the U.S. will run any talks it convenes between Kyiv and Moscow. For its part, the Kremlin views the White House as a geopolitical rival and its natural negotiating partner – while seeing the EU as a hodgepodge of individual European countries increasingly hostile to Russia but still playing a supporting role to the U.S. at best. Against this backdrop, if Europe wants to make its voice heard, it will need to wrestle with two significant challenges. [Europe] will need to maintain a united front concerning the war as the choices it faces become more difficult and consequential. First, it will need to maintain a united front concerning the war as the choices it faces become more difficult and consequential. Recent debates over such matters as whether to seize frozen Russian assets , the pace of Ukraine’s EU accession, aid packages and energy sanctions against Russia have highlighted the divisions within the bloc. Unity could be tested again as a result of political change in influential countries such as France or Germany, both of which are witnessing the ascent of right and far-right parties that could raise objections to the bloc’s support for Ukraine. For the reasons discussed below, the prospect of Ukraine’s EU membership will engender fiercer internal contention as it draws nearer. Secondly, the EU’s member states will need to reach consensus on how to approach Moscow. Positions toward Russia vary widely within the EU, from those favouring greater engagement to those strongly opposed to reopening political channels. The furore caused by European Council President António Costa’s cabinet’s outreach to the Kremlin in July showed how deep the rift runs among member states. It also did not go unnoticed in Moscow. Whether a European diplomatic track gets off the ground remains to be seen, but if it does, it would likely be led by France, Germany and the UK. Their ability to shape negotiations would depend in part on coordination with the bloc and access to its economic levers. If EU member states can align on how and when to use those levers – which include the ability to offer sanctions relief, release frozen Russian assets and support Ukraine’s reconstruction – both the lead negotiators and the EU will be better positioned to meaningfully defend European interests if and when talks get under way. Ukraine and EU Membership Meanwhile, Ukraine continues to look toward the future, particularly to its goal of EU membership. In the spring, Zelenskyy pushed for accession in 2027, irritating officials in Brussels, who felt that his tone was too demanding given Kyiv’s slowness in making the reforms required to advance its candidacy. To be sure, Ukraine has seen progress on its file in the year to date. Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban’s defeat in April parliamentary elections removed the EU’s staunchest opponent of Ukrainian membership, while also paving the way for the release of a €90 billion loan and the opening of negotiations over two areas of needed reform. Yet even with the Hungarian veto gone, the path to accession is strewn with obstacles. These include a number of fundamental concerns. Many states worry about the implications of absorbing Ukraine’s large farming sector for other agricultural states. Almost all are concerned about the budgetary burdens that would be created by Ukrainian accession, given Kyiv’s enormous financial needs and the fiscal challenges that the bloc’s members – including France – are facing. There are also bilateral disputes, such as with Poland over historical memory, that could affect the bloc’s cohesion. Another set of issues concerns how hard to press Kyiv on reforms. In December 2025, the EU and Ukraine published a plan setting out ten rule-of-law and anti-corruption measures to be taken in 2026. None is yet fully complete. Because of the Ukrainian government's go-slow approach to these politically sensitive changes, many EU officials worry that it may be counting on a shortcut to accession. Finally, the EU needs to consider how Ukraine's accession would proceed if the war were to go on for years or if parts of Ukrainian territory were to remain under Russian occupation following a settlement. Both scenarios raise complex questions, including how EU law would apply to territories outside Kyiv's control and what security obligations Ukraine’s EU membership would entail for other member states. For all the challenges, however, the EU has little choice but to make as much progress as it can. Brussels made the prospect of accession a central part of its strategic response to Russia’s invasion. It therefore needs to keep a credible path to membership open while coaxing Kyiv toward the reforms that will be required and engaging in public diplomacy to make clear its commitment to this project. Though a solid majority of Ukrainians supports joining the EU, disillusionment with the bloc could grow as expectations of a quick accession are dashed. This risk needs to be carefully managed. Against this backdrop, the EU and its member states should: Help Ukraine meet its financing needs in 2026 and 2027. The mounting economic cost of the war is placing an increasingly heavy burden on Ukraine’s public finances, even as its defence needs remain acute. With Von der Leyen and Zelenskyy having identified the resources needed to cover Ukraine’s remaining budgetary and defence needs for 2026, the EU and its member states should ensure their timely disbursement. They should move quickly to allocate the €45 billion scheduled for 2027, consider frontloading funds within the year as required and start planning now for any additional budget gaps. They should press other G7 partners, including Japan and Canada, to contribute their share of the money Ukraine will need for 2027. The EU should also urgently accelerate preparations to provide emergency humanitarian aid over the coming winter – including generators, mobile warming stations, wastewater treatment and other assistance – to mitigate the effects of Russia’s targeted attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure. It should make contingency plans to increase assistance if the situation in Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities deteriorates significantly. Direct EU defence financing toward Ukraine’s most urgent military needs. The EU should ensure that the €60 billion defence component of the Ukraine Support Loan can respond to Ukraine’s evolving battlefield requirements. Where urgently needed capabilities – like air defence systems and interceptors – cannot be obtained from Ukrainian or European producers in sufficient quantities or quickly enough, it should allow for procurement elsewhere, as it has done by permitting Ukraine to use EU loan funds to purchase U.S.-made Patriot interceptors. Meanwhile, member states should continue supplying critical capabilities, including air defence systems and interceptors, from their own stocks where possible, while EU financing and procurement instruments help expand production capacity in Ukraine and Europe. Closer cooperation with Ukraine on the development and production of drones and counter-drone systems, drawing on its extensive battlefield experience and technological innovations, should be a key part of that effort. Pursue back channels with Moscow. A fully unified EU position on how to deal with Russia is unlikely. Member states should nevertheless work toward a minimum consensus on the purpose of communication with Moscow and possible channels for engagement. The goal would not be dialogue for its own sake, but instead contacts to facilitate de-escalation, test whether openings for serious negotiations exist and prepare the EU to play a meaningful role in shaping an eventual settlement. Prior internal coordination on how and under what circumstances to deploy the levers the EU has at its disposal – for example, the lifting of sanctions – will be essential if and when substantive negotiations begin. As noted above, if a European diplomatic track emerges it is likely to be led by France, Germany and the UK, with the bloc wielding its leverage in a supporting role. Prepare for Ukraine’s EU accession in a way that accounts for continuing conflict or occupation. The EU will need to sustain its commitment to Ukraine's accession. It will need to work with Kyiv to advance reforms, including on the rule of law and anti-corruption. It will also need to prepare internally for the impact accession will have on the bloc’s budget, agriculture and institutions. Finally, Brussels should factor in the possibility of a prolonged stalemate or unresolved conflict, including continued Russian occupation of parts of Ukraine’s territory after a settlement, when planning for the country’s accession. For example, if Ukraine remains at war, there will be questions about how the bloc’s mutual assistance obligations operate alongside whatever security guarantees European states and other partners put in place for the country. Or if Russia continues to occupy Ukrainian lands, Brussels will need to consider how EU rules and standards apply to a divided territory. A credible path to membership that takes these contingencies into account would help make clear that Russia cannot determine Ukraine’s European future through perpetual war or by maintaining its occupation of Ukrainian territory. Adapting EU Foreign Policy to a World of Recurring Crises eschelhaas Thu, 10/15/2026 - 17:11 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List President's Take / Europe 15 October 2026 10 minutes Adapting EU Foreign Policy to a World of Recurring Crises Faced with geopolitical upheaval and shifting relations with major powers, the EU must adapt its foreign policy. In her introduction to the EU Watch List 2026 – Autumn Edition , Crisis Group President & CEO Comfort Ero assesses how the bloc can strengthen its capacity to address recurring crises. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print "> Download PDF Full Report (en) Comfort Ero President & CEO https://twitter.com/EroComfort Related Tags Multilateral Diplomacy European Union China United States The European Union’s foreign policy is going through historic upheaval. Like many others around the world, the EU and its member states are striving to keep up with increasingly volatile geopolitics, a profound shift in relations with the United States and an increasingly assertive China. In dealing with these challenges, the bloc and its members have followed what is becoming a familiar playbook – preserving military ties with Washington as long as possible while seeking greater autonomy and forming closer partnerships with other powers. For Brussels, the success of this strategy is likely to require progress in two key areas. The EU will need to achieve greater security and defence integration, a big task for a union of 27 governments at a time of rising nationalism, but not an impossible one. It will also need to adapt its foreign policy machinery so that it can more effectively turn its collective weight into meaningful action. Seeking a Foreign Policy on the EU’s Terms President Donald Trump’s approach to international relations – which European governments tend to see as erratic, revisionist and sometimes hostile – has accelerated the EU’s pursuit of greater strategic autonomy. That pursuit has its roots in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which caused a spike in the bloc’s threat perceptions concerning Moscow. But the EU’s sense of vulnerability became even more pronounced when Trump returned to office and began undermining the transatlantic partnership in word and deed, including by rattling his sabre at Greenland, cosying up to Russia and launching an elective war with Iran at great cost to the global economy. The U.S. has also piled heavy pressure on its European and other allies to assume more of the cost burden for their own defence. Against this backdrop, EU member states have reached consensus on strengthening their defence industries and reducing their overdependence on U.S. weapons and military technology. They have started committing substantial resources to these long-term endeavours. In parallel, the EU has also begun devising a more independent foreign policy. To be sure, Brussels and Washington have never been in lockstep on a number of key matters. The former never endorsed the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq (though some member states sent troops). It also sought to preserve the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement after the first Trump administration withdrew. Yet alignment has been more the rule than the exception. The EU long sought to nurture its ties with the U.S., while the U.S. supported efforts to make the bloc more integrated and effective. Past administrations in Washington backed EU enlargement as a means of anchoring Central and Eastern European countries in Western institutions and the transatlantic alliance. They also used Washington’s influence to forge common approaches to common challenges. Following Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, for example, the U.S. pressed the EU to adopt sector-wide sanctions against Moscow. In Trump’s times, and particularly during his second term, Europeans have increasingly come to see U.S. politics as in direct conflict with European interests. But in Trump’s times, and particularly during his second term, Europeans have increasingly come to see U.S. politics as in direct conflict with European interests. The EU has been very careful about the battles it fights with Washington, which remains its most important partner, but it has seen the need for more freedom of manoeuvre when positions diverge. As European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen underlined in her State of the European Union speech on 16 September, “building an independent Europe that has the power to act” has become a top priority. Such words are not just rhetoric. After years of talk about a “geopolitical EU”, the bloc is beginning to act like one. Increased support for Ukraine in battling Russian invaders, closer ties with Canada (itself caught up in a trade war with Washington) and successful resistance to Trump’s designs on Greenland suggest a shift in the EU’s ambition. Others are noticing. Polling in 2023 found that majorities in China, India, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and Türkiye regarded the EU’s policy toward their countries as broadly indistinguishable from that of the U.S. By 2025, the proportions had switched: more respondents now believe that the EU is an actor in its own right. Meanwhile, precisely as the EU tries to loosen its dependence on the U.S., it must also contend with a more assertive China. Its longstanding description of Beijing as partner, competitor and systemic rival has allowed governments with different interests and dependencies to avoid choosing a common course. That is getting harder. A new EU-wide threat assessment takes a sharper view of China’s ties to Russia and its efforts to shape the international order, while cheap Chinese exports threaten European factories and jobs. France and Germany are now pressing for stronger trade defences, though these could invite retaliation from Beijing. On the other side of the ledger, a number of policymakers worry that the EU’s latest trade agreement with China, in which Beijing agreed to halve its hybrid car exports to Europe, could take the urgency out of efforts to develop tougher measures. The timing is awkward: after years of U.S. pressure on Europe to take a harder line on China, Brussels is doing so just as Washington seeks to ease tensions with Beijing. A Middle-Power Moment? Over the last few years, the EU has also sought to give substance to the “middle-power moment” bruited by Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Davos in January. Brussels hopes to turn shared unease with big-power politics into a capacity for collective regional and global action by middle and other powers around the world. To this end, European Council President António Costa convened the “ Partners for Multilateralism ” summit during the 2026 UN General Assembly in New York – working with co-sponsors Australia, Barbados, Brazil, Canada, India and Kenya. An op-ed co-authored by Costa and the Brazilian, Canadian and Kenyan heads of state argued that cooperation is “not an act of idealism” but “a necessity”. The authors also expressed confidence that multilateralism could survive this era of big-power competition, though they did not explain exactly how. For its part, the EU has spent the last two years trying to build its own networks and influence through new kinds of partnership . For decades, the EU fashioned its relationships around trade with its large, lucrative market and, for some, the prospect of membership. Now it is looking for security partners. Since 2024, the bloc has concluded twelve “ security and defence” arrangements with counterparts in Europe, North America, Asia and the Indo-Pacific as well as in Africa. These cover areas like maritime security, cyber-security, countering disinformation, conflict prevention and crisis management. In principle, they also grant parties access to an EU defence financing instrument called the SAFE loan . Some in Brussels are entertaining arrangements that could go even further. Commission President Von der Leyen announced in September that she supports the idea of making Canada an “associate member” – a status that does not exist under current EU law, and is not an immediate option for Canada, but rather reflects the symbolic effort of drawing Ottawa closer to the bloc. This improvisational proposal, however, underscores a broader, recurrent question for the EU. What can it offer by way of benefits to non-members – aside from free trade agreements – that would make deeper forms of association mutually attractive, while retaining for members a core of responsibilities and privileges that come only with joining the club? At the same time, EU member states must face the reality that middle-power partnerships are not a full answer to the challenges they are facing. Overlapping alliances (sometimes likened to an armadillo ’s armour) can help preserve middle powers’ freedom of manoeuvre in some circumstances. Their interests will not always align, and even when they do, their pooled capacity will not be sufficient to address every situation. For political, economic and security reasons, many if not all member states as well as Brussels (similar to many others around the world) will find themselves continuing to depend in important ways on the U.S. and China – the very powers they are trying to hedge against – for quite some time. In the meantime, working to reduce that dependency is an increasingly important, indeed essential, endeavour. As Crisis Group has argued elsewhere , actors such as the EU can and should look for ways to work creatively with middle powers to help defuse crises, tame regional rivalries and sustain and reform international institutions, including those that are under pressure from the big powers. The Need for Internal Change There are other changes that Brussels will need to make if EU foreign policy is going to be fit for purpose in a world of recurring crises. Divisions among EU member states or EU institutions often delay or block action, which is hardly surprising given that the EU treaties leave capitals largely in control of foreign and security policy. Most decisions in this field, moreover, require unanimity. Yet as Europe faces increasingly grave threats, paralysis or delays of this nature carry a mounting price. Debates about EU foreign policy reform have therefore become more urgent. Some governments argue that, with global politics so unsettled, the time is not right for these discussions. Yet there is little to suggest that a better moment is coming any time soon. Several topics belong at the top of the agenda. First, member states need to forge greater consensus on how to coordinate crisis response and their work to meet gathering threats. A forthcoming European Security Strategy could be a starting point. Member states should work on sharpening proposals that have circulated for a European counterpart to NATO’s Article 4 (a mechanism for forcing consultations on serious incidents below the level of armed attack) and a European Security Council that could discuss matters relating to common defence and rearmament ( various formats are under discussion ). Both could speed up joint response, whether by all 27 members or in wider groupings that include partners like the UK. But any changes that are made will be useful only if they fill gaps in EU and NATO arrangements; the danger to guard against is that they do little more than add a layer of superfluous meetings. Secondly, there is a very strong argument for narrowing the requirement for unanimity in foreign policy by making greater use of so-called qualified majority voting. Under such a system, winning a vote would require a favourable vote of at least 55 per cent of EU countries, representing at least 65 per cent of the total EU population. This reform would, among other things, help prevent a single member state from blocking action to extract concessions on an unrelated issue. (Hungarian leader Viktor Orban often used this tactic before he was voted out of office, but others have resorted to it as well.) EU treaties already allow for limited cases in which foreign policy decisions can be taken in this way, for example the appointment of EU Special Representatives. Ahead of the EU foreign ministers’ informal meeting in August, eleven member states signed a letter supporting a move to widen its use and encourage more “constructive abstentions”. While several governments remain understandably wary that these changes would make it difficult for them to protect core interests, the bloc’s constitutive treaties already provide that any member can cite vital reasons of national policy to halt a vote and refer it to EU leaders for unanimous decision. But further political commitments and additional safeguards would be needed, to ensure that the bloc’s leaders continue working to reach consensus even if the change is made. The EU must preserve its diplomatic reach, staff and expertise ... to sustain its capacity for preventive diplomacy, crisis management and mediation. Thirdly, farther-reaching ideas for institutional reform deserve debate. France and Germany have proposed strengthening the EU High Representative’s office and integrating parts of the EU’s European External Action Service (its diplomatic corps) into the European Commission. The proposal has encountered pushback , and triggered turf battles, but it has also started a useful debate about whether the bloc’s current diplomatic configuration is optimal for policy formation and crisis response. Whatever structure emerges from this discussion, the EU must preserve its diplomatic reach, staff and expertise – and an ambitious budget – to sustain its capacity for preventive diplomacy, crisis management and mediation. As Crisis Group has argued previously, in today’s era of hard power, military strength and diplomatic capacity should be treated as necessary complements, not competitors. Yet the Council Presidency’s opening proposal for the next round of budget talks would cut EU foreign policy and development aid by 17 per cent against the Commission’s initial plan, weakening precisely those capacities. Finally, the EU will need to remain open to flexible arrangements that can allow individual member states to act even where there is insufficient unity for the bloc to act together. Coalitions of the willing, sometimes joined by like-minded partners outside the union, can move policy forward in some cases. Such groupings have already proven valuable in responding to Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine – particularly in putting forward possible forms of security guarantee that the bloc itself cannot provide. Similar formats could be used elsewhere, though care will be required to ensure that they bolster rather than hollow out common EU foreign policy. The Urgent and the Important The EU, which was conceived at a specific moment in European history, must adapt to the times and reorganise itself. External threats to its military and economic security can serve as catalysts for deeper integration and nimbler collective action. A new level of energy, urgency and political will appears to be mobilising for this purpose – and that is good news indeed. But some things cannot wait. The world teems with crises that will need attention from Brussels while it is putting its house in order. As always, this edition of the EU Watch List highlights an incomplete selection of conflicts both near and far where EU member states have immediate stakes or the capacity to make a positive difference. This autumn’s list includes Russia’s war in Ukraine, the explosive situation between Ethiopia and Eritrea, Lebanon, Thailand-Cambodia border tensions, and violence in the Amazon. While the EU cannot by itself resolve these crises it can – as the following entries explain – play an important part in defusing and de-escalating them even as it focuses on improving its ability to act.
